subsubtopic: TABLING OF "SUCCESS IN THE WORKS"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 32(2), I have the honour to table in the House in both official languages this Government's labour force development strategy entitled "Success in the Works".

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am veiy pleased to rise this morning pursuant to Standing Order 33 to inform the House of the Government's new labour force development strategy.
A few moments ago I tabled two documents entitled "Success in the Works", a policy paper and a background paper on Canada's emerging workforce. These docu ments outline the policy and the rationale behind the labour force development strategy.

This strategy, Mr. Speaker, is aimed at preparing Canadians for the labour market of the 1990's so as to ensure that they will be able to adapt to an evolving work environment.

It is our goal to encourage in Canada a training ethic within the private sector. We will do this through a national skills development advisory board to provide us with guidance on the needs of the private sector, by increasing funding for greater human resource planning and selected industries and sectors and occupational associations and individual firms by doubling the funding for the industrial adjustment service which helps workers and their companies face technological change, major expansion or closure, and by increasing funding for the Community Futures Program which is now helping 201 small communities plan their own solutions to counter changing market conditions.
Through the labour force development strategy we will place a greater priority on entry level training by taking immediate steps to improve the apprenticeship program, quadrupling our support for co-operative education, and designing a new program for entry level training in emerging skill requirements.

We are also asking the provinces to match increased federal funding for programs which provide job skills training for social assistance recipients and so improve the job prospects of an additional 20,000 people on social assistance.

Another area where the Government can help unemployed Canadians is through the Unemployment Insurance Program. We intend to shift its focus from one of passive support to an active response built around training and job readiness. Unemployment insurance recipients will now have access to training programs and employment and counselling services earlier in their claim. Funding under Section 26 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the fundamental training tool of the.pro-gram, will be doubled. Unemployment insurance claim-

April 11, 1989
Statements by Ministers
ants with viable business plans will be able to capitalize their benefits to help defray business start-up costs.

When older workers lose their jobs, they face a much more difficult time returning to the workforce. They will benefit from the programs I just mentioned and from increased funding to employers who hire and retrain displaced workers.
We also intend to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to make it more equitable, so that it reflects the changing work patterns of Canadians and responds to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

We will be proposing amendments to provide more flexible sickness and maternity benefits, more generous parental benefits, and extended coverage for the growing number of Canadians who choose to work beyond the age of 65. At the same time, the Government will be addressing fundamental concerns about the Unemployment Insurance Program.
The current minimum qualifying requirements in Canada's Unemployment Insurance Program will be extended from 10 to 14 weeks, to 10 to 20 weeks, depending on regional unemployment rates. In areas where unemployment remains high the qualifying period will not change. Also, we will eliminate the current repeater provisions to improve access to benefits for seasonal workers. However, we propose to increase the penalties for workers who quit without just cause, refuse a suitable job or are fired for misconduct.
Finally, the Government proposes to strengthen considerably the penalties for fraudulent use of the UI program by claimants and employers. Let me assure Hon. Members that there is no question of removing the unemployment insurance safety net for those who truly need it. At the same time, Canadians want a program and particularly the unemployed want a program that helps workers move back into the workforce.
The labour force development strategy will integrate income support for employment services with labour market programs and it will encourage greater private sector involvement. I will be tabling in the House the necessary amending legislation on the Unemployment Insurance Act in late June. I am confident that Member-sof both this House and of the Senate will study it with great care and will provide Government with their advice
and support. Until that time, I will be continuing to consult with other partners, with business, with labour and with provincial Governments, all of which have a share in the future of the opportunities we are trying to build, on how we can best help prepare Canadians and help Canadians prepare themselves for the changes that are coming in the workplace of the future.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1984 and again in 1988 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said he would not cut social programs, that social programs were a sacred trust. Today, once again, the Prime Minister has broken his word with this savage attack on the unemployment insurance system.
The Government is taking $1.3 billion out of the unemployment insurance fund and has not said how many workers will be affected, how many will lose their benefits, how many will go without unemployment insurance, and it has not said what regions will be most hurt by this policy. It is interesting to note that between 1984 and 1989, employment and training programs were cut by 30 per cent by the Government, from $2.2 billion in 1984 when the Liberals left power to $1.5 billion this year, 1989. That was a reduction of $700 million.
This morning the Minister announced that she is putting $800 million back into training programs, almost the same amount her Government took out during the last five years. Over the last five years, the Government created a severe problem in the area of training and skills development and now it is fixing this problem by going back to where we were in 1984. Unfortunately, the major difference and the great inequity in this plan is the manner of paying for these training programs.
In the past and up until today, labour market planning, development and training was paid out of the general tax revenue because these programs benefited the whole community. Now they will be paid for out of the unemployment insurance fund; that is, by the workers and by employer contributions. What does this mean? It means that all workers will pay for training without any assurance that they will benefit from that training. It means that labour-intensive industries will subsidize training for high-tech industries which are often capital intensive. It means that the slow growth regions of Canada will help subsidize the high growth regions. Workers in Atlantic Canada will help subsidize the development of high-skilled training in Toronto, fore-xample. It means that low-paid service workers will help pay for the training of high-tech workers.
April 11, 1989

Under the present unemployment insurance program, workers and firms pay into a fund knowing that the money will come back to them in the form of benefits if they became unemployed, sick or pregnant. Now, under this proposal, they have no assurance that the money paid in will come back to them in their own regions.
For example, according to the program, $230 million will go for a national skills development advisory board. That is a good thing. It is a board that will give advice to the Government on skills development. However, I would have thought that this would have already been done by the civil servants in the Minister's own Department. This probably means that the Government will be rehiring the people who gave that advice in the past but who were fired, laid off or let go, but they will be paid with unemployment insurance fund money rather than general tax revenue.
Let us look at the $65 million for human resource planning. Again, it is a very good thing, but should that not have been done over the last four or five years? Once again, money will be used from the unemployment insurance fund, money that was available for workers when they were laid off, to pay for human resource planning within the Department of Employment and Immigration.
This proposal raises many questions which are unanswered. For example, will the Unemployment Insurance Commission control these new programs that come under the unemployment insurance program including resource development, the futures program and the like? Will they fall within the ambit of the Commissioners of the Unemployment Insurance Commission? What about part-time workers, a growing percentage of the workforce? How will they be affected by this policy?
A more serious issue is the half-baked approach to this proposal. It is half-baked because it is a proposal to take unemployment insurance money and use it for training skilled workers, but there is no policy to insure work for these workers and no policy to ensure that the work is more equitably distributed in all regions of the country. A labour force development strategy must be combined with a full employment policy, with an industrial strate gy, with an effective regional development policy, a
Statements by Ministers
policy for research and development and a policy for post-secondary education. The program announced this morning says nothing of those things.
It is interesting to note that only a few years ago during the last Parliament, through Bill C-96 the Government again savagely cut back on assistance for post-secondary education, programs which go in the same direction as training programs that are talked about in this policy. The Government will train workers, but it is not sure how they will benefit or how they will find employment. Will there be jobs for them in places other than the Golden Horseshoe area around Toronto? How will we ensure that these workers who will be trained will find jobs?
We must recognize that the great growth in jobs since 1984 has been in the service sector where there is low pay, no unions and low benefits. What does this program do for those workers, particularly for those who work over 15 hours a week and must pay into the unemployment insurance fund? Those numbers are growing. How will they benefit from this program? It seems to me that these workers will be subsidizing others' training programs.
Nor has the Government explained how those who are cut off unemployment insurance will pay for their groceries and rent while unemployed. It is clear that the Government is shifting this burden to the provinces, but it has not yet consulted with the provinces with respect to this program and it has made no commitment to the provinces to help them pick up this burden which will have to be covered by the social assistance programs of the provinces.
This is another example of Tory flimflam politics. Before the election, the Tories had the deficit under control and were spending money like profligate children. They promised $22 billion in commitments in the pre-electoral period. They spent over $100 million in the Lac-Saint-Jean byelection. They poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Manicouagan riding in the years prior to the election. They did this with the biggest tax grab in Canadian history. Now, all of a sudden, after the election, there is a crisis with the deficit. Who is the first to pay the bill? It is the Canadian worker and his unemployment insurance fund.

April 11, 1989
Interparliamentary Delegation Report
Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said, and I quote, "There is absolutely nothing that will prevent the Government of Canada from maintaining all its social programs, all its regional economic expansion programs, absolutely nothing! We absolutely will maintain all our social programs in full."
Mr. Speaker, once again, the Prime Minister has forgotten his promises and attacked Canadian workers with this policy of cutting unemployment insurance.

I make a commitment today that we in the Liberal Party will fight against this plan with all the resources at our disposal. The Government is in for the fight of its life!

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. We in this House of Commons have just witnessed one of the largest thefts in Canadian history. After the last election, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised Canadians they would be protected from the worst effects of free trade. The Government promised it would provide adjustment and training programs for people who lost their jobs. Well, the Dalton Gang of Brian and Michael and Barbara have just strapped on their six-guns and ridden into town to loot the Unemployment Insurance Commission vault.
Canadian workers do not object to paying their UIC premiums because they know it is an insurance policy and insurance fund that will guarantee them some dignity if they lose their jobs. With this program, this Government is robbing Canadians of that dignity. The Department has admitted that many Canadians will lose 10 weeks or more of benefits, even in places where unemployment is 10 per cent. Thousands of Canadians who can claim unemployment insurance today will not be able to after this program is passed. Thousands of Canadians will see their claims expire and be forced on to welfare, which will be an additional cost to the provinces of this country.
What is the Minister doing with the money she is looting from the unemployment insurance fund? Well, she is going to make more money available for parental benefits. The Government deserves no credit for this. It is being forced into this by the courts, not because itwants to or thinks it is right. It proved that when it appealed the court's decision to grant parental benefits.
The Minister says they are going to use some of the money to encourage "the training ethic in the private sector". Why should unemployed people pay for an enhancement of the training ethic in the private sector? It is the failure of the training ethic in the private sector that created the problem of work shortages in the trades. Training ethic in the private sector, indeed.
The de Grandpre report had some ideas about encouraging training in the private sector. It called for a levy-grant system which would force business into injecting some of its own money into training. But this Government will never do that, not when it can steal money from working people. It is putting more money into what it describes as helping social assistance recipients.
I come from the Province of Saskatchewan where it seems this whole idea was hatched. I have seen how the government program works. What the Government is really talking about is forced labour, work for welfare, work or starve. Who are these people? They are the Canadians least able to protect themselves and most deserving of Government help.
I can tell this House that the raid on the unemployment insurance account is only the first raid. In the Department's report, it says:
Changes to the way the unemployment insurance program is
financed will be announced by the Minister of Finance in the
forthcoming Budget.
That means the Government will stop paying for regional extended benefits. It will be shifting billions of dollars worth of costs from Government contributions to premium contributions. In other words, it will be taking its deficit reduction off the backs of working people as well as its training programs.
This is a betrayal of the working people of Canada, and there is no way that the New Democratic caucus can support this.

I rise today to introduce a Bill asking that April 28 of each year be designated as a day of mourning to honour all persons killed or injured in the workplace.
If this Bill passes we will recognize both the enormous numbers of people who are injured or killed while at work, and the great need for a new emphasis on health and safety in the workplace.
According to the latest Labour Canada statistics, one million people are injured in the workplace each year. Deaths from injury average nearly 1,000 each year.
Statistics for deaths that occur because of exposure to unhealthy working conditions are unavailable, because such deaths go largely unreported and uncompensated.
It is my sincere hope that the passage of this Bill will focus Canadian attention on the real need for greater workplace health and safety.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to humbly present to this House a petition from my fellow citizens who humbly declare that at this time, there is no law in Canada to protect the lives of unborn children from conception to birth. Because they believe in the sanctity of human life from conception, they also believe in the necessity of a just law to safeguard the right to life of the unborn child and the right to be protected while it grows until it is born. They believe that it is our duty to protect life and they also believe in faith in our future and that this can only be guaranteed by showing respect for life, from the unborn to the elderly. They also believe that families and other groups or communities have the duty to develop various forms of support and shelter to assist future mothers in need. They humbly ask Parliament to draft and pass a law to protect life from the moment of conception, a law that would seek to save the life of the mother and the child at the same time.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to join in the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I would like to speak about the agriculture industry in Canada since I believe that there is profound unease and concern with respect to exactly where the Government is going in terms of agriculture. The concern may have stemmed from the free trade deal which the Government passed last December and in commitments which the Government made with respect to removing oats from the control of the Canadian Wheat Board.
There is also concern with respect to the promise the Government made last November 10 concerning the provision of $850 million for drought payment. Most of those payments will not arrive until well beyond the seeding period this spring.
There is profound concern in the agriculture community with respect to exactly where the Government is going in all these areas. But perhaps the greatest concern is with respect to the question of free trade and the GATT negotiations. In looking at the document entitled: "Speech from the Throne" most farmers will find very little comfort. There are only three lines in it to suggest where the Government is going with regard to agriculture. It is stated in the document:
Canada's efficient agricultural producers cannot compete fairly in a world in which trade-distorting subsidies wreak havoc with market disciplines, while bringing undue pressure to bear on the nation's treasury.
Surely, the Government should have more than this to say about the state of agriculture in Canada. It is interesting that one of the themes in the Speech from the Throne is " A Strong Economy". Yet there is no reference to agriculture in terms of that strong economy, even though 17 per cent of Canadians are involved in agriculture or the food processing industry in some way.
Under the theme "Preparing Canada's Future" there is no reference to Canadian agriculture. Under the theme "Jobs for Canadians" there was no reference to agriculture. I can understand why the Government did not want to discuss agriculture under this theme since just about a year ago there was a report that some 25,000 jobs in agriculture had been lost in the previous 12 months in western Canada alone. How much the figure is for the whole country is anyone's guess.
Under the theme "The Environmental Imperative" there is no reference to agriculture. Nor is there a reference to it under the theme "A Caring Nation". That is probably the greatest tip-off that the Government does not care and that it is certainly not concerned about the agony faced by thousands of Canadian farm families in terms of their debt and other problems.
Thus we are left under the theme "Canada's International Role" with the three-line reference to agriculture. Yet part of it is devoted to the suggestion that agriculture and farmers are an undue pressure on the Canadian Treasury.
The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) announced out of the blue a few months ago that he was removing oats from under the control of the Canadian Wheat Board. That has to be one of the most damning decisions that any Minister has ever made. He certainly has been damned for it.
There are some 24 Canadian Wheat Board advisory groups across western Canada, groups which are elected by the producers themselves. It is interesting to note that at some 22 of the 24 public meetings held by the advisory committees it was demanded that oats be reinstated under the Canadian Wheat Board marketing system. It is also interesting to note that at 10 of the meetings it was demanded that the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds be replaced.
One can see how effective the Minister has been in persuading these 24 advisory committees across the West that his decision with regard to oats was a good one. Clearly, this has to be some type of a pay-off to those in western Canada who are opposed to the Wheat Board. They are smaller groups but they have been opposed to it for years in terms of orderly marketing. This is clearly a pay-off to the big multinational grain companies who want to see the small exporters and the small individual operators out of the business.
It is interesting to note that as members of my caucus held a number of meetings across western Canada with the grain producers it is not now only the small individual farmer who will be hurt by this decision but small private enterprise exporters who will also be hurt since they will now have a secure supply of oats to export into the special niche markets in the U.S. This is something which they now have. We will actually lose this type of orderly marketing.
April 11, 1989

In Oak Bluff, Manitoba, at the producer committee meeting some 117 voted to see oats remain under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board while 46 voted to have it removed.
Yet if we consider a place such as Wapella, Saskatchewan, we see that some 85 of those attending the Wheat Board Advisory Committee meeting voted to have oats reinstated-zero voted to do what the Minister wanted to do.
Clearly there is great unhappiness and concern with the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds and his cavalier method of removing oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board with very little support from the producers themselves. I have not heard anyone say that his approach was the right one especially since he did not consult with the prairie pools or other farm groups. Of course, he was soundly condemned by the pools as well as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which, in a resolution, demanded that oats be maintained under the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board.
This document does little to reassure farmers of exactly where the Government is going. The Government may argue that it did not really want to spell out its neo-conservative agenda until after the Newfoundland election. This only creates more concern for farmers. The Government will not spell out exactly what it is doing with agriculture until later because of the political fall-out from Newfoundland or other parts of the country. So we have to wait until the Budget comes down later this month.
I believe that there is great concern as well regarding the Government's direction with regard to marketing boards. We argued during the election campaign that marketing boards would be incompatible with the free trade deal because when you remove tariffs on processed foods, it is not possible for the Canadian processing industry to compete with processed foods coming in from the U.S.
Clearly that is exactly what is happening. The Grocery Products Manufacturing Association met recently with some members of our caucus and said,"We simply cannot compete, we told you this before the election, we told you this before the free trade deal went through and we are telling you now that the Government has to get rid of marketing boards or we will have to move our processing industry to the United States."
The Address-Mr. Foster
I am sure that the strategy of the Government is to blame the grocery products manufacturers and to blame GATT for the destruction of the marketing boards.
We believe that that is a real threat. Clearly when you look at the de Grandpre Report, that is the direction in which they are heading. They are saying that we should establish a two-price system for our farm products, marketing commodities like poultry, turkey eggs and the dairy industry. If it is impossible to establish a two-priced marketing system, then they suggest that the quotas be increased. Mr. Speaker, that scenario will ultimately see the destruction of the whole marketing system which, I understand, farmers in Europe and the United States admire very much. They would like to have a system where they are paid on the basis of their cost of production, a formula price which guarantees them an adequate return for their investment, for their labour, for their management. It is a system which has served Canadian agriculture very well.
I suggest that if we hadn't had controlled commodities in dairy and poultry during the past three or four years when prices have been very low for many other farm commodities, the scene would have been much worse than it is today. But clearly the signals coming out from this Government, from the de Grandpre Report, from GATT are that the Government has put the whole question of farm marketing boards, Chapter 11 of GATT, on the negotiation table. Only time will tell, but certainly the signals are very bad.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is significant that the President of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Don Knoerr, in a press statement on March 29, condemned the de Grandpre Report. He said in his press statements:
It appears that the only concern expressed by the Council was that Canadian processors must be allowed to obtain their raw product at a price comparable to that in the United States.
He went on to say:
It is hard to understand how the Advisory Council on Adjustment could, after listening to a few briefs from the processing sector, could conclude that the concerns raised by the Tariff Board were irrelevant, and that no consideration had to be given to measures that may be necessary to maintain a viable horticultural sector in this country.
Clearly the de Grandpre Commission Report was simply to say, we have to look after the processors, not the farmers, that is their problem. So I do not think, Mr. Speaker, there is a very great concern with where exactly this Government is going with regard to national farm marketing boards in this country.

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Foster
I want to speak as well, Mr. Speaker, about the farm debt situation. Last year the agriculture committee made a number of recommendations with regard to this country's farm debt situation, and yet there was no reference at all to it in the Speech from the Throne. Our report last July indicated there was a $6 billion debt which could not be financed under current available Farm Credit Corporation programs, and yet in the Speech from the Throne we hear nothing.
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture put out a press statement a couple of days ago calling on the Government to be more concerned about the farm debt crisis. It pointed out that only $83 million of a $160 million fund established to assist farmers had been used, that only 253 Ontario fanners out of 1,148 that had gone before the Farm Debt Review Boards had received assistance, in spite of the fact that in 1988 farmers suffered a severe drought, hog prices were veiy low and interest rates increased dramatically.
We have seen very little action by the Government with regard to the debt situation in this country. We are now facing some of the highest real interest rates in the history of the country. With a 4 per cent inflation rate and a bank rate approaching 14 or 15 per cent, we are looking at real interest rates of around 8 to 10 per cent. Farmers cannot operate with real interest rates at that level.
So we are disappointed that the Speech from the Throne makes no provision for the farm debt situation, no new provisions for the very high interest rate that farmers face this year. The drought assistance will arrive too late and simply will not be of benefit to many producers. Furthermore, the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program, which was announced with great flourish last fall, has not been made available to farmers. Fanners have said that it has been one of the most confusing programs ever. Farmers were asked to make their application by March 15, but many of them had not received their application forms.
The headlines in many papers described the difficulties faced in that regard: "Drought Aid Assurances Ring Hollow for Farmers", "Drought Pay Disappoints". Those are just a few headlines from farm papers. Other headlines include: "Politicians Hear Drought Aid Frustrations", and, "Drought Aid Battle Drags On". Thew-hole situation is untenable for agriculture in this country.
Therefore I want to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Vanclief): That the following words be added to the Address:
This House regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recognize the importance of agriculture to Canada's economy:
(1)	by only making a three-line reference to agriculture in the Speech from the Throne implying that farmers are a drain on the national treasury;
(2)	by removing oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board without consulting with, or obtaining the approval of, the major farm organisations thereby adding to concerns that the Board will eventually be dismantled;
(3)	by taking a position in the Free Trade negotiations which will lead to a weakening, if not the destruction, of Canada's orderly marketing systems in the grain, poultry, dairy and horticultural sectors, and by not providing adequate adjustment programs as evidenced by the de Grandpre Report;
(4)	by failing to commence negotiations with the U.S. on an agricultural subsidy code so that farmers will not face U.S. countervail at the whim of U.S. lobby groups such as is now threatening Canada's pork producers;
(5)	by undermining the viability of the beef industry by allowing increasing amounts of "no roll" (ungraded) beef into Canada from the U.S.
(6)	by not providing any new initiatives through the Farm Credit Corporation to cope with the farm debt crisis and high interest rates;
This amendment sets out our concerns with the Speech from the Throne and the lack of action by the Government in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today to address my colleagues in this House. Of course, the subject of my participation is the debate on the Speech from the Throne delivered by Her Excellency, the Governor General.
In order to participate in this debate, something which I clearly wanted to do, I had to go through a rather intensive job interview, much like all of us here in this House, for a period of some 51 days. I was in competition with four other candidates. In the end, the residents of Ontario riding, the voters, chose me as their voice here in this House.
As a new Member of Parliament for Ontario riding which is made up of the three municipalities of Ajax, Pickering and Whitby, it has been my displeasure to listen to those members of the Opposition here in this House, members of provincial legislatures across Canada and reactionaries across Canada continuously attack the prosperity that we in central Canada enjoy. Yes, my riding, Ontario, is sharing in that prosperity.
I could raise numerous responses to all of those reactionary comments, but I think it is sufficient to point out that during the last four years, Conservatives from Ontario supported the Government in its actions to correct the injustices foisted upon the regions of Canada by the Liberal Government of the previous 16 years.
More significant, however, is the point that when the Liberals were in the process of destroying the fabric of Canada during the 1970s and the early 1980s, Conservatives from Ontario sang a common refrain with Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament from across Canada in opposition. We were the only national Party speaking for Canada. Now, this Speech from the Throne reflects the continuing reality: the Progressive Conservative Party is still the only national Party.
I have listened to my colleagues on the government side relate the good things in the Throne Speech that will be received by their ridings back home. It comes as no surprise to me that the constituents of an Ontario riding have a very similar perspective. During the recent election campaign, I talked about the problems of the deficit, even if my opponents did not want to. In fact, they made spending promises as though we did not even have a debt, never mind a deficit.
April 11, 1989

At a recent public forum I had with my constituents less than two weeks ago, 80 per cent of the people present wanted the Government to reduce the deficit, to make programs more responsive to those areas in need and to take whatever steps are necessary to accomplish that goal. Yes, central Canada is very active, but I think it rather naive of people to think that inflationary pressures in central Canada will not affect them in their regions.
I would refer Hon. Members to an article in this morning's financial section of the Globe and Mail. It deals with a report by Statistics Canada, and I would like to quote one paragraph from it: "The price of new houses in Vancouver rose faster in February than in any other major city in Canada including Toronto, Statistics Canada reported". I caution all Hon. Members, if they think they are immune to inflation, to watch out.
Just ask the fireman, the policeman, the electrician, the steelworker or any other unionised employee if they are prepared to work for less in your part of Canada when the negotiation process they believe in and participate in clearly uses comparisons to lever their salaries up. Ask the banks, the civil service and corporations which have offices across Canada how difficult it is to promote people who live in the regions because they cannot afford to bring them to Ontario. Do you really believe that people in my riding with large $100,000, $150,000 or $200,000 mortgages can afford high rates any better than people in other ridings, or that small business in an Ontario riding is not affected by the bank rate? Of course it hurts, but at least this Government is trying to do something about it.
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the Liberal Government of the day did nothing but spend money while mortgages increased or rose to 20 per cent and 21 per cent levels. All they did was spend, spend, spend, while farmers were evicted, businesses of all kinds went broke and homes were repossessed across Canada.
Need I remind this House of the infamous Finance Minister from Cape Breton whose Budget in the early 1980s was so bad that it had 49 amendments within months and was soon thereafter cancelled? His reward was to lead the Liberals in the Senate. The deficit must
The Address-Mr. Soetens
be reduced, and the Speech from the Throne clearly indicates that it will be.
In Ontario riding, we have very low unemployment levels. It hovers around 4 per cent, yet as can be witnessed in the local media, there are numerous jobs available. I have a copy of one of the newspapers distributed in the local media. It is called the News Advertiser. It is not known for its job opportunities advertising, but I have four pages of ads listing jobs that are available. Let me read some of the jobs that are available in my riding. This is just a sample. A nuclear medicine technologist; a landscape carpenter; a landscape maintenance foreman; kitchen staff and preparation cooks; journeymen; millwrights; management trainees; financial analysts; sales secretaries; drivers; production workers in the marine industry; menu clerks; hair stylists; receptionists; telemarketers; machine operators; accounting manager; assemblers; photographers; journalists; maintenance mechanics; electricians; mechanics. There are jobs for students. There are jobs for mature people. There are full-time jobs. There are part-time jobs. There are even jobs available, subject to retraining, for members of the Opposition when they are defeated in the next election.

Living in an urbanized area next to a big city brings with it many unique problems relating to the environment. All those industries create air pollution. All those people create garbage. We have always recognized our obligation to help the less fortunate both at home and abroad. The Mulroney Government shares in these values. Ironically, that is why the deficit is so important. We must address it to ensure our ability to maintain the quality of our social programs in the years ahead. That is why, despite our financial problems, we will continue to provide assistance to families and the elderly while directing greater assistance towards those with low incomes.

I can only reiterate that a statement made by the Minister of Employment not too long ago addressed successfully the concerns raised by the Hon. Member.
With regard to abortion legislation, I can only refer to the previous legislation which was rushed and hurried. Ultimately, the Supreme Court decided that it was flawed. I can only hope that when and if the Minister brings forward legislation it will be appropriate and that it will not be taken to the Supreme Court and proved to be flawed but that it will stand the test of the laws that are appropriate at the time.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to comment on the Throne Speech pronounced last week.
First of all, I want to say this is a very vague speech, although during the week we started receiving more specific information, this morning for example, when the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDou-gall) introduced a number of changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which are actually quite welcome, with a few exceptions.
Before commenting any further on the subject, I would like to say that I support the stand taken by my Leader (Mr. Turner) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that the notwithstanding clause in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is in direct conflict with the spirit and the intent of the Charter. The House will recall what the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa, did in that province just before Christmas, when Bill 178 impinged on the Anglophones' freedom of speech, specifically in the area of bilingual signs. I know what I am talking about, since Quebec Anglophones have been denied that freedom. I am also very concerned as a Franco-Ontarian. However, I want to express my appreciation to the Peterson Government in Ontario for its recent statement that it would never impose that kind of legislation on Franco-Ontarians.
The Address-Mr. Belair
In the Throne Speech, the Government also made some allusions to reducing the deficit. Although they were just, I am very wary of any measure that will be taken to reduce this deficit. There are no specifics. There is a reference to budget cuts. I think we will just have to wait until the bills are introduced in the House, to find out what to expect.
The Government has again made a commitment to earmark certain sums of money for regional development.
If I may go back somewhat in time, the FEDNOR Program was announced in the spring of 1987. I imagine it was a calculated coincidence that we started seeing the colour of that money in the North only a few weeks before or at least not until the month preceding the election in November 1988.
At that time, $100 million was granted over a period of five years, which means $20 million per year. So far we have yet to see any of the $20 million the Government promised us. We are very aware of our isolation, being far from the main urban centres where the economic action is, and we in Northern Ontario intend to make sure we get our share of the pie, in order to help our small businesses.
There was also a reference to subsidies or grants or economic assistance for Native people. I wish the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Cadieux) would visit the reserves in the North and the Arctic and see for himself the conditions in which these people have to live. I will talk about housing later on in my speech.
During the last ten years, we have been talking about political autonomy for Indians. Political autonomy is possible only if Native people are economically independent from the rest of Canada. The potential for economic development exists, but these people do not have the necessary financial resources to develop that potential within their own culture and in their own language, while still living in a cultural context they understand.
I spoke earlier about unemployment insurance, and this morning the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) proposed a number of major changes. There are some positive aspects I would like to mention, especially assistance for older workers who are likely to have trouble finding employment, depending on the economic situation where they live.

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Belair
Once a person has reached a certain age, it is always difficult to retrain for another job, and the Minister was right to help these people. Where I would like to make a few suggestions is on the subject of fraud. Mr. Speaker, everybody knows there are unemployment insurance profiteers who abuse the system, and the solution would be to appoint more investigators to track them down and bring them before the courts. The suggestion aimed at lengthening the qualifying period for entitlement is not necessarily good: keep in mind the handicapped, people who are not overly talentuous, or others who may be slightly retarded and you will appreciate that these applicants would certainly find it difficult to qualify for unemployment insurance.
The Minister should also consider the case of seasonal workers. To be more specific, an employee must work at least 15 hours a week to be covered. At the end of 20 weeks that employee would qualify for unemployment benefits, having worked 300 hours. What about someone who works 10 hours a week, 52 weeks a year yet does not qualify for benefits with a total of 520 hours of work? I feel that is an injustice which ought to be eliminated by the Government.
The Speech from the Throne refers to environmental matters, and it is obvious that popular pressure has struck a responsive chord in the Government. Suffice it to mention extremely positive aspects concerning toxic chemicals, the quality of our drinking water, and ozone layer protection; the idea is to protect the atmosphere and shield people who inhabit the Earth from harmful sun rays. Our forests is one sector where the Government has fallen short. All one needs to do is fly over Canada's northern expanses and see the ravaging effects of acid rain: ever more reddish spots, our evergreens are turning red because they are being choked by acid rain. Extremely important steps certainly could be taken in that direction. Suffice it to mention in passing that the forest industry is the largest employer in Canada, with one million directly or indirectly employed, a fact which should warrant the Government giving it a little more respect and priority.
Since I am on the forest industry, Mr. Speaker, let me send a very important message to this Government-it concerns the effect of the 15 per cent export surtax slapped on the lumber industry. In February 1989, the Northern Ontario Liberal caucus visited a number of cities. We heard 30 people who made representations on the impact of that surtax on the lumber industry. Let me
say only that right now, in Northern Ontario only, five sawmills are shut down. This has meant the loss of 900 jobs, and a number of industry owners and managers told us that currently, a number of mills are operating at a loss or at cost. Combining the exchange rate now estimated at 15 per cent on the Canadian dollar relative to the U.S. dollar, and the surtax, we see Mr. Speaker that the industry is operating with 30 per cent less income than it was on December 30, 1986, when the tentative agreement was signed with the U.S. Trade Department.
I think the Government is extremely aware of the importance of that surtax. Since the damage has been done, would the Government not consider repealing that tax, with the 30-day notice provided for in the Free Trade Agreement, and let the Americans take their countervailing action, that is go before the GATT and attack that tax.
The industry has clearly shown that it too would be ready to help eliminate this tax, even with the aid of an international tribunal, as was suggested to us during our hearings. Surely it cannot be worse that the present situation. We have everything to gain by eliminating this tax.
A few moments ago, my colleague spoke about abortion. I fully agree with what he said to the effect that the Supreme Court a few weeks ago. . . and I would have much preferred that it render a decision on the Borowski case to establish once and for all whether a fetus is a human person from the moment of conception. In my mind, there is no doubt about it, but since we have to live in a country where the Supreme Court is the final authority on any dispute, I am prepared to wait, but I expect the Government to take the necessary action to prevent abortion on demand.
Mr. Speaker, we could also talk about what is not included in the Speech from the Throne, especially the Canadian Government's approach to the U.S. Commerce Department regarding the definition of a subsidy. Everyone knows that this definition will have a major impact on the whole Canadian economy. If the Americans consider a subsidy for small Canadian industries or small businesses to be unfair competition, can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the impact that will have on our country? We are only 26 million people. Obviously, the number of companies is proportional to the population of Canada compared to the United States and we have an extremely big country geographically. There are wide open spaces between the towns and villages of our land.
April 11, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the problem of transportation in Canada. Many industries are subsidized for the distance goods have to be shipped, in order to remove any regional disparities that might exist.
Let us also talk a little about housing. In his budget cuts-which have already begun, by the way-I am referring here to RRAP, the Rural Rehabilitation Assistance Program, the former Minister of Housing, whom I see across the aisle, did not see fit to give more money to help poor people repair their houses and renovate, especially in isolated regions.
I just spoke about native people. As far as housing is concerned, one has only to visit remote reservations to see the atrocious conditions in which these people have to live. I am convinced that no one in Canada deserves such a fate and that more money should be given to Indian reservations so that they can provide proper housing for their residents.

subsubtopic: REQUIREMENT FOR LONGER QUALIFYING TIME IN AVALON, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my statement concerns the requirement for people in the Avalon region of my riding to have 16 weeks of qualifying time for unemployment insurance benefits increased from the normal requirement of 10 weeks due to the regulations that cause certain things to happen when the unemployment rate drops below 11.5 per cent.
Notwithstanding the Government's new labour force development strategy that was tabled here this morning, my concern and that of my constituents is that the qualifying time has increased while the employment opportunities have not. Of the three UIC regions in Newfoundland, the Avalon region is largely driven by the employment opportunities in the urban area of St. John's. Specifically, the unemployment rate there is in the order of 8 per cent while in other rural parts of the region the rate is more than double, approximately 19 per cent. Yet all recipients are being treated the same. They require 16 weeks instead of 10.
Those outside St. John's have enough trouble obtaining 10 weeks. How can they now be expected to get 16 weeks? They are being devastated.
I have written the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) in more detail and her staff would be aware of this concern.
May I ask the Minister in the strongest terms that the Avalon UIC region in Newfoundland be separated immediately into urban and rural so that UIC recipients in the rural area where unemployment continues to be high can be treated more justly and fairly and in consonance with the employment opportunities available.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to urge Canadians to celebrate National Wildlife Week, April 9 to April 15, by taking part in conservation activities across Canada.

April 11, 1989
National Wildlife Week was proclaimed in 1947 to raise awareness about the problems affecting wildlife and its habitat and it is just as applicable today. In recent years, many private organizations have joined with Gov ernments to focus public attention on the threats facing wildlife by organizing such activities as nature workshops, wilderness trips, film festivals and special exhibits.
Although the challenge to reverse and prevent damage to our precious wildlife heritage is daunting, the task is one in which Canadians from all walks of life can participate. I urge Canadians everywhere to join with a local conservation organization and participate in wildlife conservation activities throughout the year.
Let us do all we can to make every week wildlife week in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, last week in Timmins another miner was killed on the job. This accident is the second such tragedy in the same community in the last two months. While safety remains an overriding problem in this industry, the Government's attitude has been unacceptable.
At the upcoming meeting of the federal and provincial Mines' Ministers, the stated first priority for discussion is to be "maintaining the competitive edge".
I call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to give the mines portfolio a Minister of State for Mines so this important area will receive the attention it deserves. I call upon the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) to change the agenda for the August Mines Ministers meeting so that safety for mine workers becomes the priority of the Government. I also call upon all Members of the House to support the Private Members' Bill introduced today by my colleague, the Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), calling for a national day of mourning for workers killed in the workplace. Workers' lives should not be allowed to pay for corporate profit.

Mr. Speaker, our miners have no use for yet more studies. The research has been done and the recommendations have been made. Now is the time to act responsibly and protect the health and safety of Canadian miners. The Government should give top priority to safety in the mines.
Action is what is needed, Mr. Speaker!

Mr. Speaker, animals have been used for centuries as living tools for the achievement of human knowledge. An estimated two million animals a year are used for research in Canada.
Although there are areas of medical research where animal testing might be necessary, many uses such as testing cosmetics, furniture wax or paint cause unnecessary pain. Animals too often suffer for questionable human gain.
It is unacceptable for animals to be sacrificed for our vanity and it is time that we asked ourselves if the end justifies the means.
I urge the federal Government to encourage research by finding alternatives to senseless animal testing where possible.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want to bring it to the attention of Hon. Members that I am obliged to make sure that statements stay within the 60 seconds as set out in the rules.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the annual report he has just tabled, the Official Languages Commissioner sounds the alarm in connection with bilingualism at Canada Post: under the privatization program of the Conservative Government opposite, franchise operators offer postal services and this is a threat to bilingualism at Canada Post Corporation. The Official Languages Commissioner tells us that the least we could expect would be to have franchise operators sign contracts and make formal commitments with Canada Post with a view to providing bilingual services.
Better still, Mr. Speaker: Why not do away right now with the postal service privatization scheme so that once and for all we would be sure of bilingual services at Canada Post, just as it has always been the case? That is the only solution to the Canada Post bilingualism pro blems.
April 11,1989	COMMONS

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House that this week is National Soil Conservation Week.
Canadian farmers know that good soil is an important element in producing the quality food products for which Canada is famous. The Government is to be commended for establishing programs such as the Soil and Water Environmental Enhancement Program. This program will assist in reducing the phosphorus loadings in the Lake Erie Basin from cropland run-off and improve the productivity of southwestern Ontario agriculture in reducing or arresting soil erosion.
On behalf of the agricultural community in Elgin County and Norfolk Township, I would like to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) for their foresight. This initiative will ensure that future generations will have productive land to farm and will be able to continue producing Canadian farm products that are wholesome and of high quality.

subtopic: INQUIRY INTO IMPACT OF OIL EXPLORATION URGED
INQUIRY INTO IMPACT OF OIL EXPLORATION URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 23, there was a major oil spill off the Washington coast which seriously impacted on the West Coast of Vancouver Island. On March 28, an even more serious oil spill took place off the coast of Alaska, and the effects are still unknown.
On April 5, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) turned down a request for an inquiry. I am asking him to reconsider in view of the fact that at this very moment a press conference is being held in Vancouver where a committee representing some 158 prominent British Columbians are asking in a letter addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for a full inquiry into the environmental and social impacts of the exploration, production and transportation of oil and other dangerous substances in Canadian coastal waters. I ask the Minister of the Environment to reconsider in view of this interest in the Province of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, on March 30 last, in the presence of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), Her Excellency the Governor General of Canada, Mrs. Jeanne Sauve, bestowed on Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel, Chief Electoral Officer of Canada, the Outstanding Achievement Award, the highest award in the Federal Public Service. Under Mr. Hamel, was appointed on June 6 1966, the Canada Elections Act has undergone a positive evolution.
Mr. Speaker, we also appreciate the competence of the impressive team he heads in Ottawa. On behalf of all Elections Canada employees and of all Parliamentarians,
I would like to pay a special tribute to Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel and to offer him my most sincere congratulations.

Mr. Speaker, cold fusion could well revolutionize the energy production and utilization on our planet if this process can be proven and commercialized. The importance of the current research on cold fusion, should it prove routinely verifiable, cannot be exaggerated and would surpass any previous scientific development in history.
The successful development of cold fusion would minimize environmental problems and radically change world political and economic influences now exerted by major oil producers.
My contacts with Canadian and American researchers indicate that many are becoming believers. Two possible pathways of reaction have been identified.
With our vast freshwater supplies and heavy water technology, Canada should be on the forefront of possible development.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CUTS IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
EFFECT OF CUTS IN GOVERNMENT SPENDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the critic for the Canadian International Development Agency, I like many other Canadians hear persistent rumours that major cut-backs

April 11, 1989
will soon be imposed on government spending. After this morning, we tend to believe it more. These cuts include Canadian aid for Third World development.
I appeal to the Government to do everything in its power to ensure that international aid, particularly that directed to Africa, the poorest of continents, is spared if the Government does in fact reduce its budgetary expenditures. Consider these facts: Per capita income in Africa is lower today in real terms than it was 30 years ago. Between 1979 and 1983, life expectancy declined in nine countries of the sub-Sahara. With regard to education, primary school enrolment has fallen in 12 countries. Surely these people can be made an exception to this lean and mean Government.

maintopic: TRIBUTE TO THE HON. ROBERT STANFIELD
TRIBUTE TO THE HON. ROBERT STANFIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, April 11, is the 75th birthday of a former distinguished Member of this House and distinguished son of Canada, the Hon. Robert Stanfield. My first recollection of Robert Stanfield is from the provincial election of 1956 where as a young student, I was sent to cover the inevitable re-election of the then Liberal Government of Nova Scotia. I got there too late because Bob Stanfield, having taken over the Party eight years earlier with no members provincially or federally, had achieved a victory.
Bob Stanfield's career would have been complete had he never left Nova Scotia, but in 1967, he accepted the unhappy and difficult task of national leadership. Through three difficult elections and nine years, he re-built this national Party into the central institution it has become today. His unswerving integrity and commitment to full equality in terms of language rights and social justice, his progressive approach to leadership, his belief in the reconciling of regions and of making this an important place for the debate that would make this country viable has contributed much to the public life of Canada. Today we salute a great Canadian on his 75th birthday.

Mr. Speaker, this Government is not a caring and compassionate Government, it is a callous and careless Government.
Via Rail links this Confederation from the East Coast to the West. For many thousands of Canadians, the rail lines through their towns or cities are a symbol of how vast this great country is and how yet we are all Canadians. The Government was callous when it brought up the idea that Via Rail would be cut in the upcoming Budget. Families across the nation wondered if there would be a pink slip waiting for them the next day.
The federal freight rate subsidies are vital to the Atlantic economy. We need these subsidies to transport our goods to market and distribution points in central Canada. We cannot afford to lose 12,000 jobs.
This is a careless Government. Uncertainty at the national level with regard to the continued funding of economic development programs has created chaos among the workers and businesses of Atlantic Canada.
Cut-backs in Via Rail, the Atlantic freight rate subsidies and the Economic Regional Development Assistance Programs appear to be on this Government's agenda. Via Rail, the freight rate subsidies and ERDAs are essential to Atlantic Canada and must be maintained.

subtopic: COURT JUDGMENT ON THE RAFFERTY-ALAMEDA PROJECT
COURT JUDGMENT ON THE RAFFERTY-ALAMEDA PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it ironic that today, the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark) rose in his place to talk about National Wildlife Week while remaining silent about a judgment rendered on the Rafferty-Alameda project, a judgment that was brought forward as a result of an action taken by the Canadian Wildlife Federation, a judgment which showed that the federal Government did not live up to its responsibilities with respect to a federal environmental assessment on the Rafferty-Alameda dam, a judgment which has quashed the licensing of that dam.
April 11, 1989

Oral Questions
I now call on the Government to correct the error made by the former Minister of the Environment, and I call on the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. L. Bouchard) to live up to his responsibilities, not to appeal the decision, to initiate a federal environmental assessment review and to ensure that Saskatchewan does not defy the law of the land and proceed with this project regardless of the court judgment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. The Tory Government has not launched an attack on poverty, today it launched an attack on the poor. It has not launched an attack on unemployment, today it launched an attack on the unemployed.
Canadians who honestly and legitimately find themselves out of work or lose their jobs are having their benefits cut by $850 million. Why should a Canadian who, through no fault of his or her own, loses a job, pay for human resources training by big companies? Why are unemployed people, who have to feed their children and pay their rent, pay for training programs in Canada? Why is the Government forcing unemployed people onto welfare to pay for what should be government training programs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is, of course, wrong on all counts. We are ensuring that people who are unemployed continue to have benefits. Yes, we are saying that they will have different kinds of benefits. We are ensuring that they will have access to training and that they will have the possibility of having secure jobs in the future. We are paying for the kind of training that they will need to have those jobs. That is a better kind of benefit than staying at home when most of them do not want to stay at home.

subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the issue is who is paying for the training. Under this plan, the unemployed will be paying for the training.

subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is taking money from the unemployed to pay for retraining people who already have jobs. Is the Prime Minister going to pay or the Minister? Certainly not! Quebec's textile workers and British Columbia's forestry workers are going to pay. Why should workers who don't have enough money for their rent, clothes and food, have to pay the cost of retraining programs? Why should people who have enough problems of their own, and are unemployed, be made to pay for the cost of retraining others, which is the Government's responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I think retraining is the responsibility of all of us because it is the future of Canadian workers that we in this Government are concerned about. The right hon. gentleman is always talking about doom and gloom, but for every story that he can come up with about gloom and doom, I can point to a Canadian who has benefited as a result of the Government's economic policies, and under this program, they will benefit more.

subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so much for the Prime Minister's undertaking that our social programs were a sacred trust. So much for his statement made during the debate among the three Leaders, particularly his response to the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), that all our social programs would survive the trade deal. So much for his promise during the election campaign that Canada would have the finest adjustment programs in the world for our labour force. All that has gone by the board. Why did the Prime Minister not tell Canadians the truth if this was going to be the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: RE-TRAINING PROGRAMS-RESPONSIBILITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are making this program a better one, and I do not understand why the Right Hon. Member would suggest that this program is being cut. The size of this program remains the same. The people who are unemployed will now have access not only to income support, but under the training programs in the UI program, programs which are not a new phenomenon but whose funds are being doubled, they will get income support, transportation allowances, child care and the cost of the training program. What could be better for unemployed Canadians than that?

April 11, 1989
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: LOSS OR REDUCTION IN BENEFITS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
This morning, we had a preview of the Budget which indicated that nearly one million Canadian workers will lose their unemployment insurance benefits, either altogether or partly, as a result of the program announced by the Minister today.
Does the Minister agree with these indications, and if not, what are her own predictions? And is she prepared to produce publicly, here in the House, her own impact study on this issue?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: LOSS OR REDUCTION IN BENEFITS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
The Government of which this Member was a part did change the entrance requirements under unemployment insurance. We did not invent this. This has been done before. This time it was done in a way that those people will have access to other programs. When his Government did it, it simply extended-reduced the ability of people enter the program. We are saying those people will have access to a secure job and a secure future.
The Hon. Member is saying a million people will be affected. I do not think that number is right. We have been sensitive to regional disparities so people in higher unemployment regions will continue to have access to the program at an earlier date.
We have also eliminated the repeater provision put in by that Government. We made it easier for these people to find a job and to find training. We brought our programs together in a continuum for employed and unemployed to ensure that our workforce in the future has the greatest security of job opportunity in the world.

subsubtopic: LOSS OR REDUCTION IN BENEFITS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

asked the Minister to produce her impact studies to show us how many people will be affected by this program. She has not answered that. We want those impact studies.
The Government announced it was taking $850 million out of the Unemployment Insurance Fund by reducing benefits and redirecting moneys to training, labour market development and consultation, worth-while activities, but all matters that in the past were paid for out of general revenue because they benefited all Canadians.
My question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration is this. How can the Government justify this radical attack on the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and what will it do to assure Canadian workers across this country that moneys they have paid into that fund will be returned to them in benefits or training in their own provinces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: The Hon. Member has clearly missed the point because that is exactly what will happen. We had in the past a mixture of programs under the Unemployment Insurance Program and under General Revenues that provide training and benefits to workers. That will continue. What we will do is double the effort under the Unemployment Insurance Program and under the Canadian Jobs Strategy, which remains whole. This is a change from their policies whereby they make work; we make jobs!
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext: We are reinforcing a positive direction recommended by a committee of this House that unemployment insurance become more active.

No matter how the Minister deals with the issue, the question that workers will be asking right across the country is: "Who will pay for the retraining involved?" Is it the unemployed themselves, as the Government wants to do, or is it those who can afford to pay for retraining programs? That is the issue.
My question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. What she did amounts to taking $1.3 billion out of the Unemployment Insurance Fund, out of the pockets of the unemployed, a direct or indirect tax on them. Why didn't the Minister, as her buddy Ronald Reagan has done in the United States, institute a minimum corporate tax on profitable companies? She could have raised over a billion dollars there and taxed those who could afford to pay, namely, the corporations that are making money, for these changes, instead of the unemployed themselves.
April 11, 1989

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
The Leader of the New Democratic Party is singing the same old song. He sings it on every issue. A billion dollars from corporations is supposed to pay for everything.
Let me say that premiums paid into unemployment insurance are paid by employers, as well as employees. It is a benefit to employees who are unemployed or may be unemployed in the future that we will see people changing jobs more often. The Hon. Member knows that. There is a different kind of benefit going to the unemployed now. It is one the unemployed have asked for. They want training and secure jobs. They are ready to pay for them.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext: The Minister has learned her lines well. Every question she is asked today about who will pay for this, she turns around and talks about retraining. No one on this side of the House is arguing against retraining. We are saying the unemployed should not have to pay for that themselves! That is the issue.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
The Minister is smiling. She is not the one looking for a job.
Why is it the United States can afford to have a minimum corporate tax and other industrial countries can have a minimum corporate tax on profitable companies, and this Government would rather tax the unemployed? Why don't you bring that tax in and do the just thing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext: It is both employed people and corporations that pay for unemployment insurance. It is not the unemployed. The unemployed do not pay for unemployment insurance.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Both companies and employees pay into the Unemployment Insurance Fund in order to have access to the benefits of the program. We are shifting the benefits of the program in a way that is more positive and will ensure workers in the long run will have access, not just to money to stay at home, but money to go out and get another job.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: FORECAST CUTS IN PROGRAMS-GOVERNMENT'S PRE-ELECTION COMMITTMENTS
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only three minutes left, and I find it rather difficult to get back to my subject, the Throne Speech, after such a long pause. Nevertheless, I would like to raise a number of points. I would have liked to see the Throne Speech deal with the problem of air safety, and more specifically at Toronto's Pearson International Airport. When you travel by air every week and have this nagging feeling that you might not be able to land or your plane might have a mid-air collision, it should be enough to make the Government and the Minister of Transport make this very serious problem one of their top priorities.
Also absent from the Throne Speech was any mention of the purchase of nuclear submarines. I don't think Canada needs them. What good would a few nuclear submarines do if we are stuck in a cross-fire between two world superpowers, the Americans and the Russians? Since we don't have any other form of military support, what good would these nuclear submarines be? The money could be better spent.

In conclusion, may I reiterate my disappointment at the total exclusion of the forestry issue from the Throne Speech, considering that the industry employs a million people in Canada and the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber is a very serious blow to its viability. It is extremely urgent that the Government was initiate a new round of negotiations with the United States to eliminate this devastating tax. It is of the utmost importance that the federal-provincial agreements on forestry
resource development be renewed. Forest regeneration is the future of the industry. Access roads to reach mature timber must be constructed.
The Government should be praised for creating an independent Ministry of Forestry. Now it should live up to Canadians' expectations.

speechtext: Questions or comments? No questions-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the opportunity to ask my colleague a question or two. At the outset I want to congratulate him on a very fine speech. He certainly has distinguished himself in the House in the very short time that he has been here. His commitment is not matched by anyone in the House when it comes to matters affecting his particular jurisdiction.
The Member has spent considerable time analyzing the Speech from the Throne. We on this side of the House have been very critical of what has been missing from the Speech from the Throne.
The Speech from the Throne is supposed to outline in principle the general thrust, and general programs of the Government for its mandate for at least this, the Second Session of the Thirty-fourth Parliament. Needless to say, as my hon. friend has pointed out, the Opposition and Canadians generally have been terribly disappointed by the general thrust and direction the Government will have us take.
We noticed today, for example, that the Government appears to be more concerned about the deficit than the lives of Canadians and Canadian families from one end of the country to the other. There was very little mentioned in the Speech from the Throne about the Government's intention to be so brutal in dealing with the deficit.
Is it any wonder that Canadians throughout the country call into question the integrity and honesty of that particular Party and the Government when, during the election campaign, the Government through the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a number of different promises to Canadians? We heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) say today that they did not make very many promises during the election campaign. It was quite laughable to listen to the Minister of Finance say today that the Government did not make many promises. It leads one to ask: When is a promise a promise?
April 11, 1989

During the election campaign the Minister of Finance said that they were simply election commitments and not promises. We can imply from his comments today during Question Period that because they were not promises, somehow the Government is not bound by the commitments it made to the people of Canada during the election campaign last fall.
My question concerns the Government's integrity and honesty. There is no doubt that my colleague's Conservative opponent in his riding made a lot of promises during the election campaign, no doubt duplicating the promises made by the Government itself. Will the Hon. Member comment on some of the promises that were made by his Conservative opponent in his riding and comment on the Finance Minister's statement today that not very many promises were made? Do his constituents feel, as mine do, that the Government is totally lacking in the area of integrity and honesty?
