speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, a number of promises certainly were made during the election, concerning for example, regional development. The House will remember that in the Spring of 1987, the Government announced the FEDNOR Program. It only took a year before we finally received some moneys from the Government, and by a well-designed coincidence, some projects were accepted only one month before the general election. The intention no doubt at that point was to prove to people in Northern Ontario that a Conservative Member would be more acceptable than a Fiberal Member, but I am sorry to tell them that the Conservative candidate was beaten, and by quite a margin!
During the campaign, the Conservative candidate also recognized that the 15 per cent export surtax on softwood lumber was harmful to Northern Ontario's people and forest industry. If we agreed on one thing, that was it. I am not sure whether that candidate was speaking on behalf of his party, but he fully recognized it-anyway the three candidates fully agreed that tax is harmful. We saw the results-five sawmills have shut down since the agreement was signed. There was a loss of 900 jobs, without the governments, then and now, doing anything to launch re-training programs for those employees.
The Address-Mr. Belair
Going further, Mr. Speaker, I could add that across Canada a lot of small sawmills, a lot of independent owners without links to the pulp and paper industry are hurting tremendously.
The message I would like to convey to the Government is to remind the Minister of International Trade, as my colleague from Winnipeg did this week, that he should start anew very serious negotiations with the Americans to repeal that tax that will do new harm across Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Belair) on his speech. He is not only a distinguished Member from northern Ontario, but is also one of our co-critics for forestry. He has done a commendable job of outlining the problems and difficulties of the softwood lumber industry. Clearly, no industry has faced such a difficult time as has that industry in northern Ontario.
The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) suggested a couple of weeks ago that he thought it would be inappropriate to go to Washington now to negotiate. Member for Cochrane- Superior just how urgent it is for the Minister to go to Washington or for the American Secretary for Trade to meet with the Minister here in order to renegotiate this agreement. Could the Hon. Member outline for the benefit of government Members and the Minister for International Trade just how urgent this situation is?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the question of the Hon. Member for Algoma. Again I repeat that the message I have for the Government is that the Minister for International Trade should contact the American authorities at the earliest opportunity and attempt to renegotiate an extremely harmful tax.
As I said, five mills have already closed their doors. When in Thunder Bay we met with a very large group of workers who had been laid off just before Christmas. If we combine this tax with the rate of exchange of the Canadian dollar as compared to the American dollar, the

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mrs. Collins
result is that the industry must now make do with an income 30 per cent lower than it was on December 31, 1986.
Mr. Speaker, anyone can see that no single industry in Canada would continue to operate after sustaining such huge losses in terms of both profits and manpower. Now, a few words about the impact of these lay-offs. Municipalities have to hand out additional welfare benefits and the workforce is highly depressed. Remember that these people have worked hard to improve their working conditions and then, practically overnight, they are left with absolutely nothing, not even a retraining program. speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed, it is a sincere pleasure to have an opportunity to participate in the debate in response to the Speech from the Throne. First, I would like to pay my respects and offer my congratulations to the Speaker of the House who still remains the first Member ever to have been elected to that position. That is something very important to remember and should not be quickly overlooked. During this Session, while we will not agree on very many things in the House, we certainly have agreed on the unparalleled respect that we have for the Speaker of the House, the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) and indeed his Deputy, the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski).
I would also like to extend my very warm welcome to the new Members who are serving in this Thirty Fourth Parliament. Their constituents have placed great trust in them, and I am sure they will never give them any cause to doubt that trust in either their motives or their convictions. It is my sincere hope that our new colleagues will derive as much pleasure from the proceedings of this House as I have during the past four years.
It was just a few short months ago that the people of Canada reaffirmed their support for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and this Government. With the passing of the Free Trade Agreement, businesses across Canada and particularly in my home Province of British Columbia can now begin to plan for the months and years to come with the full understanding that they will not be
undermined by wilful Government interference in the market-place.
This Session will be particularly challenging and rewarding to me personally as I have been tasked with the responsibility of serving as a Minister of the Crown, Associate Minister of National Defence. I can assure all Hon. Members that they have my commitment to serve this House and all Canadians with all the vision and vigour that I can muster.
I have heard some say that perhaps my appointment as the first woman to hold a defence portfolio is nothing more than sheer tokenism. I for one certainly disagree with that sentiment. My Cabinet colleague, the former Minister of National Defence, now the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty), was in fact very important in breaking down the barriers to women within the armed forces. I am proud to carry on the work that he began after his appointment nearly three years ago. If my appointment by the Prime Minister is any indication, I would have to suggest that those internal barriers have finally disappeared. As Sir Winston Churchill used to say, this is not the end, this is not even the beginning of the end, but it is perhaps the end of the beginning.
The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal recently released its findings on an issue of fundamental importance to the Canadian Forces and for equality rights in Canada. The tribunal has ruled, as Hon. Members know, that there is no basis in law for the Canadian Forces to restrict the employment of women in either the regular or reserve forces except in submarines. This decision when implemented will open to women combat roles, both on land and at sea, roles which had previously been open to men only. I was pleased to announce on behalf of our Department that we would be fully implementing this decision over the next decade.
I want to stress, however, that the equality of opportunity for women in the Armed Forces is not a goal suddenly imposed. Rather, on the contrary, Canada has been a leader for almost 20 years in the employment of women in military service. Since 1971 when only 1,500 service women were permitted in the regular force, the numbers have risen to some 8,300 today. This represents almost 10 per cent of the current regular Force. Within NATO, Canada is second only to the United States, with
10.2	per cent of its military comprised of women.
April 11, 1989

The Department of National Defence has many proud traditions and I take much delight in my association with them, and the Minister, the Hon. Member for Kinders-ley-Lloyminster (Mr. McKnight). Together we have been deeply impressed by the professionalism and dedication of both the civilian and uniformed members of our Department. I would also like to commend both the reserve and the cadet groups across Canada who make up an integral part of our mandate. They have given me the warmest of welcomes, and they know they have no stronger supporter than I.
This Department is steeped with tradition, since the appointment of Sir Georges Etienne Cartier as the first Minister of Militia and Defence under Canada's founding Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald. I believe it is a great challenge and privilege to be the first woman to join the ranks of such distinguished Canadians as Cartier, Mr. Brooke Claxton and Major-General George Randolph Pearkes, another British Columbian who was awarded the Victoria Cross while serving as a uniformed member of the Canadian Armed Forces, and indeed our former colleague, Allan McKinnon from Victoria, whom we miss very much in this House.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Our Armed Forces are known around the world for their particular talents as keepers of peace, and we in Canada have a very proud tradition in this respect. Yesterday morning I had the opportunity to visit with over 200 young men and women gathered in Petawawa who will be leaving later this week to join the UN peacekeeping forces in Namibia. This group was excited about the opportunities they will be facing. I was deeply impressed by the dedication they were showing to this very challenging task.
As they set forth across the ocean, I want to say a special word of appreciation to them and to their families who will be staying behind. We will be watching them with a great sense of pride as they work in this difficult and challenging situation. They follow in a tradition of similar groups, Canadians who have formed part of the peacekeeping operations in the Suez Canal, in Cyprus where Canada's own Commander Milner is now in charge of the peacekeeping force, and in the Golan Heights. We all wish them a very safe journey.
Another area of our Department I have a particular interest in and wish to encourage is our civilian air search
The Address-Mrs. Collins
and rescue associations. This responsibility was transferred to National Defence in 1976 and has flourished through a much needed blanket of safety across many remote areas in this vast country. The spirit of altruism shown by the men and women who serve in these associations is a welcome sign of compassion that is often too scarce in today's society.
I hope I can bring a more diverse face to our Armed Forces. As we invite more women to train for the Armed Forces, so too should we recruit more young Canadians from different racial and cultural backgrounds. For many decades, our country has seen the increased predominance of those who were not of British or French origin. Within our Armed Forces, however, such a mixture of backgrounds and heritages is not as strong as it should be. I believe the human face of our Armed Forces should reflect the ever-changing plurality and make-up of Canada. For an institution to be vibrant and dynamic, it needs to mirror the values and character of the community it is required to serve. We have an opportunity to build on the traditions of the past, exploring and accepting new ideas and thoughts that will in the long term make our Armed Forces a stronger and fuller player in Canadian life.
While we celebrate the opening of this session of Parliament we must not overlook another milestone that we, as a country, reached this past week. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, NATO, just celebrated its fortieth anniversary, which has served as a cornerstone of our Canadian foreign defence policy. NATO was born in the aftermath of the Second World War and has continued to represent the benefits of collective security through 40 years of relative stability in Europe. NATO has been put to many tests, but the unity and determination of the Alliance has not wavered.
NATO provides a regular forum for interaction between different nations and has developed over its 40 years a very healthy economic and trading relationship. Many members of this House have participated in various NATO groups. They have talked to me about the tremendous opportunities and experience it has provided. Today, NATO provides for the common security of over 600 million people in 16 nations on both sides of the Atlantic.
If I might quote my colleague, the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark):

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mrs. Collins
The modem era is marked by conflict, yet Europe, the region with the highest concentration of sophisticated weaponry in the world, is enjoying the longest sustained period of peace and stability since the height of the Holy Roman Empire.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Thanks to NATO.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thanks to NATO. That collective success is something in which we should all take pride.
As the Prime Minister said recently, we believe there exists in Canada today a profound desire to get on with the job of preparing a better future for our children and their children. This Government was elected on November 21 to serve our nation. Last week's Throne Speech was a map for the next four years of Government. It has often been said that when you do not know where you are going, any road will take you there. The Opposition is all too familiar with taking any which road, only to end up at a dead end. Our Government has a map that will lead Canadians along the road to continued prosperity, a road map that does not circumvent or miss the important elements that are necessary to every successful journey.

Mr. Speaker, this is a tall order and an enormous challenge, but will remain vigilant in our economic and social policies. I believe it will serve the interests of all Canadians in the years to come.

Over time, many issues will be discussed in this House. My constituents in the riding of Capilano-Howe Sound will agree with me when I say that perhaps no issue is of more importance at the moment than the protection of our environment. My home province is proud to bask in the splendour of nature's beauty. We are blessed with the expanse of the Rocky Mountains, the crispness of glacier-fed streams, the abundance of animals and marine life, and the grandness of the Sitka spruce trees in the Carmanah Creek Valley. We do not take our good fortune for granted.
The recent disaster of the Exxon Valdez oil tanker off the coast of Alaska brought home the delicate balance between nature and commerce. I was pleased to participate in the emergency debate held in this very place last Tuesday evening. I said that night and will say again, that no system can ever be perfect. This Government has learned from the mistakes of others and is prepared to deal with any difficulties that should threaten the coast or islands of British Columbia. I must remind the
members of the Opposition who indicated the Government was somehow responsible for this tragedy that we on this side of the House are here for the sole purpose of representing the best interests of our constituents and to safeguard those delicate balances that contribute to the quality of our daily lives. As such, I can assure Members opposite, when I stand here and tell them that we will do everything in our power to prepare for any future disaster, that is the actual situation, plain and simple.
I too must answer to my constituents. As many of them live on the rocky shores of the Pacific or Georgia Strait, one can be sure that I am paying close attention to developments which come out of the Alaska oil spill, and the lessons that we must learn from this incident.
A concrete example of the commitment of the Government to foster economic development in Pacific Canada was demonstrated last year with the creation of a Pacific directorate of the Department of Supply and Services. On August 6, 1988 my colleague, the Hon. Member for Oakville-Milton (Mr. Jelinek), elevated the status of the office in Vancouver to that of a directorate. That means that British Columbia businesses can do business with the Government of Canada in British Columbia as opposed to coming to Ottawa. Combined with the Western Diversification Office in Vancouver, and the western procurement initiatives announced this past year, one can see that the situation is changing for the better. We can count on the determination of the Hon. Minister responsible for western diversification to bring the situation that much further to one of parity between all regions of Canada.
One aspect of the western economic development in which I have had a particular interest is that of the Asia-Pacific Initiative. This past week I was honoured to be appointed the lead British Columbia Minister responsible for this far-sighted program. It was conceptualized by our dear friend and former Minister for International Trade, the Hon. Pat Carney. With almost one year left in API's mandate, I have already begun to collect advice from the Blue-Chip Advisory Committee which includes members from the private, public, and academic sectors. The advisory committee has appointed task forces that are addressing opportunities and advising both the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia in the areas of international finance, trade, transportation, tourism, and cultural and social impacts, as well as the export of professional services.
April 11, 1989

All told, more than 100 senior volunteers from the private sector are engaged in some aspect of this operation. The Asia-Pacific Initiative has built strong links between our country and the many nations of the Pacific Rim which serve both our economic and cultural interests.
I am proud to be a member of a Government that is concerned about the long-term as well as the short-term development of our regions. We are committed to providing an atmosphere where people can be optimistic about their day-to-day lives. Our neighbours and our constituents have asked that we maintain the caring and compassionate aspects of our society. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has promised that this will be done. I can assure all Hon. Members that nothing in the Throne Speech will undermine that commitment. Our Prime Minister is committed to supporting those who are in need of assistance, whether they be seniors, children, veterans, or the handicapped. However, we cannot continue to live beyond our means without inviting disastrous consequences. That is the other message which is so important to convey to Canadians today.
I hope that my own children, who are just reaching adulthood, and all children of Canada, will be able to enjoy the same benefits and opportunities that I have had. This will be impossible unless our generation of Parliamentarians comes to the realization that we cannot continue to spend freely and mortgage the birthright of those who are yet to come. Not to act now would be tantamount to making our children economic hostages and slaves to our own largesse. We cannot allow that to take place. We need resolve and determination if we are to develop the more productive and competitive economy that we have committed to in the Speech from the Throne. We shall bring forward measures in the Budget later this month which will diffuse the ticking time bomb of growing debt, and establish a new framework for fiscal responsibility that my children and yours demand of all of us.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to congratulate the Minister on her historic appointment as Associate Minister of National Defence, and to particularly commend her for the position taken by the Government on the decision of the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal on full involve ment of women in combat positions within the Canadian Armed Forces. We welcomed that decision.
The Address-Mrs. Collins
I would like to ask the Minister about another equality issue within the Canadian Armed Forces. The Minister will recall that she was a member of the special committee on Equality Rights which reported to the Government of Canada in 1985. It unanimously recommended that the Canadian Armed Forces bring its employment practices into conformity with the Canadian Human Rights Act, as amended, to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. The Member, now Minister, concurred fully in that recommendation of the committee.
In March, 1986, the Government promised to take whatever measures were necessary to ensure that sexual orientation was a prohibited ground of discrimination in relation to all areas of federal jurisdiction.
As the Hon. Minister knows, men and women within the Canadian Armed Forces who happen to be gay or lesbian still are not accorded full equality and justice. I would like to ask the Minister to confirm that the current policy within the Canadian Armed Forces is as stated in a written answer to a question on the Order Paper which I submitted last May. The answer of the then Minister was as follows:
Current policy has been further modified in that the involuntary release, under Item 5(d) of QR&O Chap 15, of serving members actually engaged in the practice of homosexual activities has been suspended pending government consideration of the Canadian Force policy.
I would like to ask the Minister to confirm that that remains the policy of the Government of Canada. When will the Minister finally recognize the oppression and the cruelty of current policies? Men and women who are qualified and capable of serving their country have their careers in limbo, are not entitled to take part in career development programs, are not entitled to promotions, and their security clearances can be jeopardized. When will the Government finally recognize equality and justice for gays and lesbians within the Armed Forces? When will the Government finally live up to the promises that it made? When will the Minister live up to the commitment that she made as a member of a committee that unanimously recommended equality and no discrimination for gays and lesbians within the Canadian Armed Forces?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby-Kingsway (Mr. Robinson), for raising this issue on which we have certainly had discussions in the past. I recall our work together on the committee on Equality Rights during 1985 in which we discussed these issues at great length with Canadians

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mrs. Collins
across the country. That was one of the reasons that I was particularly pleased that within weeks of my appointment I was able to make the announcement that women would be allowed full access to practically all occupations and trades in the Armed Forces. That certainly reaffirmed the recommendations of that particular parliamentary committee.
Many of the recommendations of that committee caused some concern at the time. I am sure my hon. colleague will recall that. However, in the fullness of time, and it may take some time for all recommendations to be implemented, they will certainly stand in good stead. I feel very proud of the work that we did in that committee.
I would also like to confirm to my colleague that what he has said about the existing policy of the Department of National Defence with respect to sexual orientation is indeed true. Following my former colleague, the now Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty), an appearance was made at the Standing Committee on this subject. At that time he made a commitment that there would not be any involuntary release of personnel because of their sexual orientation, until there was an opportunity for a full review. This was a change from the policy which had existed earlier that involved releases in certain situations.
Since my appointment I, and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight), have been addressing this issue and asking for a review of the policy. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss it with my other colleagues. We will bring forward our report will make it known to Parliament in the fullness of time, which I hope is not too long in the future. I cannot give the Hon. Member a date, but certainly a review is ongoing and I am sure we will keep him well informed of its outcome.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I have indeed derived pleasure from the proceedings of this House. However, I have also derived pain from the Throne Speech. It will impact negatively on the poor and disadvantaged of our country.
As Associate Minister of National Defence, can the Hon. Member in fact muster, as she said, with all vigour, the scrapping of all nuclear submarine programs?
Does the Associate Minister agree that the right to live is the beginning of human right as is stated in The Hague Declaration of last month signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)? If so, will she lobby Cabinet to promptly introduce legislation against induced abortion to protect the right to life of the unborn?
Will the Minister share with the House the position of the Government as to how it will handle and help the unbearable debt that Third World countries now shoulder?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his question and I will deal with the different parts of it.
With respect to the issue of abortion, I am sure that if the Hon. Member has read Hansard over the past years he is well aware of my personal position on the matter, a position which I have held long before I was involved in politics. There is certainly no wavering from my position that this is a matter of choice for women.
With respect to nuclear submarines, I would like to give a little history on the matter. When the Government took office in 1984 we inherited a situation with respect to our Armed Forces that was utterly terrible. The morale was gone. There was no equipment. If one talked to many of the women and men who served in the Armed Forces they would have seen that it was really a dispirited group. That was as a result of 17 years of neglect under the former Government.
When we formed the Government we initiated the first review of defence policy which resulted in the White Paper on defence tabled in the House in 1987. As I am sure the Hon. Member will recall, we also introduced separate uniforms for the different commands. I must say that that has been a measure which has helped to reinstitute a great sense of pride in the men and women who serve in our Forces.
Uniforms are not enough. We cannot have soldiers, sailors, airmen and submariners without proper equipment. They do not have it. They have not had it. A major part of the White Paper looked at the equipment requirements of our Armed Forces to develop a plan to
April 11, 1989

refurbish them, to give them the proper equipment in order to do the job.
In the Navy, a number of alternatives were put forward. As the Hon. Member knows, we have the frigate program which is going ahead for the construction of a dozen frigates, the Trump program, the mine counter-measure vessels for our reserve forces and the proposed submarine program. If we look around the world we see that the navies of the world all have submarines. It has become the technology of modern navies. Yet Canada, with a tri-ocean coastline and despite 75 years of submarine service, has very outdated oberon-class equipment in the Oberons.
It was the recommendation the of White Paper and of the Department that we should embark on the construction over a long period of time-27 years-of a new, updated modem capability for our Navy in the focus of nuclear-powered submarines. As I said in the House yesterday, we are all facing the Budget which will come down on April 27. There has been a review process. Until we know what the resources will be for our Department we cannot make final decisions about the major capital purchases of a variety of items. I do want to say that the White Paper on defence continues to be the policy of the Government with respect to defence issues.
The Hon. Member asked me about our support to Third World countries. Quite honestly, I cannot think of any Government which has done more with respect to our involvement through CIDA and the involvement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recently on Third World debt issues than our Government. Our Canadian International Development Agency programs are looked upon around the world with tremendous respect. I look at the work it has done to ensure the improved role of women in Third World countries, something in which we have been a real leader in the various programs that we have developed. I look at the recent developments to decentralize CIDA, to put our people right out on the front lines so that they are knowledgeable about the needs of programs and the tremendous changes that have taken place, and the improvements in our international development programs since this Government has taken office.
I would think that the Hon. Member would want to congratulate the Government on the tremendous role it has played and the sense of responsibility it has shown toward Third World countries. This is in the interests of us all. We all know that unless we can see those Third World countries developing and providing more economic independence for themselves that in the future we will
The Address-Mr. Brewin
not have markets or good global economy. It is certainly in the interests of us all to help support those initiatives.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating you on your re-election to the Chair. You have been a great credit to this institution. It is a matter of great pride for me personally to serve in this House under your Speakership. May I also say that I appreciate very much your personal courtesy on a number of occasions already in this new Parliament.
May I also congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the Hon. Member for Calgary Southeast (Mr. Richardson) and the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mrs. Gibeau).

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Brewin
I would also like to extend my thanks to the voters of Victoria. It is a great honour to represent the community of Victoria and Oak Bay in this House. The constituency of Victoria has been represented by a diverse number of people over the more than 100 years British Columbia has been in Confederation. I suppose the most notable is the first Prime Minister of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald. All of the Members until today have been either Members of the Liberal Party or the Conservative Party. We now have representing Victoria the first social democrat. I am very pleased and proud of that.
It is my intention to share the perspectives of the people of Victoria. I should say that I think the political evolution of Victoria is only a precursor to the political evolution of the country.
Victoria has the reputation of being a tweed curtain, a rather quiet and retiring place. In fact, it is a very creative, lively and imaginative community. I suppose all of us would be inclined to proclaim the geophysical beauties of our own constituencies, but Victoria is a very beautiful place.
We have a very dynamic arts and cultural community, and have had for many years, producing some of the finest artists and musicians in the country. It is perhaps for that reason that we are particularly upset with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for its persistent failure to provide even the minimum production and broadcasting facilities in Victoria. We have had 50 years of neglect. We are the only capital in Canada which has no radio or television production services, a fact we intend to remedy in the next few years.
I have had some very useful discussions with senior representatives of the CBC. I hope that in the next few years, with the active support of the people of Victoria, we will see a change in that direction.
We are a very active sports community. We have produced champions. It is partly because of that that we took interest in bidding for the Commonwealth Games in 1994. We are very pleased that in Seoul last September, Victoria was given the honour and responsibility of hosting the Commonwealth Games in 1994.
Victoria is a community with above average numbers of seniors, partly because of its commodious climate and
its rich cultural diversity. Because of that we are in some respects on the cutting edge of a social change that all communities in Canada are going to face in the years ahead. As a result of a much higher percentage of seniors in the community, there is a need for changes in medical services, in transportation, in community services, in housing, and in policing.
As a result, we have a number of very important and innovative programs in Victoria which I think the countiy will do well to study. I particularly draw attention to the neighbourhood policing project that, with the support of the Solicitor General's Department, we are finding to be a most effective way of delivering police services in our community.
Having pointed to some of those, let me say that we are not without our problems. I suppose, in keeping with most communities outside the central part of Canada, we have particular problems with the quantity of jobs and the quality of jobs. We have persistently high unemployment and persistently high underemployment. The Minister responsible for employment was proclaiming with great enthusiasm the Government's record in job creation, but we have to look behind the numbers to see the kinds of jobs that have been created.
We in Victoria are as experienced as most other communities in Canada with the problem of low-paid, insecure jobs which do not challenge the minds and creativity of those who hold them. As a result we too suffer a drain of our young people from our community and the lack of challenge the job situation provides.
We are working ourselves on those problems, but I believe the federal Government has a major role to play in diversifying in a regional way the good jobs in this countiy and planning for the long run so that people can continue to live and work in the communities in which they grew up.
However, underlying what is generally for most people a reasonable standard of living is an anxiety felt all across this land, not for ourselves but for our children and our children's children, an anxiety about the future of this planet.
We hear on the news night after night about the ozone layer, the greenhouse effect, PCBs, oil spills, the destruction of our forests, many of which occurrences we see right around us. This fear is beginning to be reflected in the responses of all political Parties in Canada. I suggest that it is the critical issue before this Parliament.
April 11, 1989

As a result of this, I come to this Parliament with an agenda which includes a number of specific matters for the community of Victoria. At the top of the list are environmental issues, and a number of specific ones to Victoria include the requirement for land-based sewage treatment. We still pump raw sewage into the Strait of Juan de Fuca. It is a situation which all community leaders have concluded must stop. In due course we will need federal assistance to eliminate it. Studies are now under way by the Capital Regional District to see what the specific requirements are, but in due course in the next couple of years, we will be back to this Parliament and to the Government for assistance. The Government has provided assistance for Halifax. It must provide assistance in this area for communities such as Victoria.
As well, there are specific issues of economic development in which the federal Government is directly involved. I am thinking here of Ogden Point, the lands owned by Transport Canada. It will be a major source of development in the years ahead, and it will be very important for this Government to give sensitive attention to the development of Ogden Point.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, let me move to what I believe is my mandate from the voters of Victoria, to raise issues of national importance with a perspective from our community. I am going to list and try to develop in the few minutes left to me five issues: First, the environment; second, Canada's role in the world; third, issues of national unity; fourth, the questions of national economic development; and fifth, questions of social justice.
On the issue of the environment, I was struck by the references in the Speech from the Throne to the environment, but putting that in juxtaposition with some references made earlier in the Speech to the free market economy. It was as if two different people had written these two sections of the Speech from the Throne. It made me wonder whether the Government has actually read the Brundtland report.
On the one hand, the Government committed itself to the virtues of the free market economy and, second, lauded the Brundtland report. Yet, the Brundtland report is a stunning indictment of the impact of the free market economy over the last 100 years. It is impossible to achieve the objective of saving this planet if we leave economic decisions simply to the workings of the market-place. The Brundtland report states very clearly that
The Address-Mr. Brewin
there is a place for the market, but it must be overridden by the community imperative of saving the environment.
As the Government moves along the path of increased concern for the environment, I ask that the Government take its concern to its logical conclusion. As we have had the specific issues put to the House during the last 10 days, in each case the Government's response was that it would act more effectively, more quickly. In that lies the long-term strategy for coping with the environmental crisis. No one in this House could believe that if the forests of British Columbia and Canada are left to the forest companies alone to decide we will have any forests left within the next 10 years. The only way that we can preserve the forests is for Governments at all levels to intervene and ensure that they are protected.
We have other environmental issues, but rather than deal with the specific issues, let me just outline some thoughts on a general strategy. The Government must crack down on polluters. The Government must encourage an orderly transition of industries which are recognized as damaging the environment. The costs of that transition cannot properly be expected to be borne by the employees, the workers, even the individual companies that are working in an area which we now see must be phased out. We must work in a planned, effective way from an environmentally destructive economy to an environmentally sustainable one. That transition will require careful, step by step planning. It will have to involve communities, companies, and workers. Plans will have to be put into effect to have a transition. The costs of that transition must be borne by society as a whole. Therefore it will be with great interest that I will be listening to the Budget two weeks from now to see whether it is in any way integrated into the imperative requirements for saving this planet.
We are fortunate in Canada to have economic growth virtually every year. A recession is when we slow down the rate of economic growth, but that economic growth as it is presently structured is leading us to environmental disaster. We must begin to see that there can be no increase in personal wealth for the top half of the earners in this country until we bring the environmental issues under control.
The Budget must deal effectively with consumer spending of those who already have too much. It must begin to divert the economic growth we are looking at over the next number of years toward saving the environ-

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Brewin
ment and distributing the goods and services that we produce in this country in a more fair manner.
I want to speak briefly about Canada's role in the world. This is a matter of great concern to the people of Victoria. We are proud of the fact that we have one of the largest peace walks every year in this country. We are a community that is committed to peace. We want to tell the Government that the time has come, given the dramatic developments in the Soviet Bloc, for Canada to take effective and vocal leadership in exacting from the West a flexible response to the initiatives taken on the other side of the Iron Curtain.
This planet has lived in jeopardy of nuclear destruction for 40 years. We have still not moved away from that particular danger. The world is still armed with 50,000 nuclear warheads. It is of crucial importance that we take this moment in history to try to move on both sides, now particularly in the West, to break down the arms race and step back from the abyss, to reduce our reliance on nuclear and conventional weapons.
We also want to see a reduction in the reliance on conventional weapons around the world. We want to see the Government regain the initiative in Southern Africa to rid the world of the evil of apartheid. We want to see the Government finally pay some attention to the needs and concerns of the peoples of the islands of the Pacific who now suffer from living in the world's nuclear backyard.
There are also issues of social justice and national unity. We in the West believe that it is critical that we bring Canada's aboriginal people into Confederation. We agree with the concept of a distinct society. At least I know the vast majority of my constituents believe in the concept of recognizing Quebec as a distinct society as acknowledged in the preamble of the Meech Lake Agreement. However, we disagree vehemently with the Prime Minister's intemperate outburst of last week in his attack on the constitutional amendments of 1982 and the development of the Charter.
We say this is a time for patience on all sides of the House. We ask that those from central Canada and Quebec in particular, now that Quebec has reached a new maturity in Confederation, take a sensitive response and reaction to what is happening in western Canada. There is a deep sense in western Canada of being left out of the decision making.
The Government may say that that is unfair, but it is a view that is a deep-seated reality. The Government has not responded to that, including the Government of the Province of Quebec. It is not enough to dig in one's heels on Meech Lake and insist that it be passed without change. There must be an indication of flexibility.
I am proud that this is a bilingual country. I do not agree with those who say that French is being forced down our throats, but it is an attitude which must be dealt with in an understanding way. The way in which Mr. Bourassa responded in December to the Supreme Court decision fell far short of that mark.
Let me address the issues of social justice since this affects the area in which I am critic, particularly that of Solicitor General. There are issues of grave concern to all Members who are concerned about issues of social justice. They include conditions in our prisons, the conditions among our native people, the loneliness of people who are aged, and the grotesque division of wealth in this country. Some people struggle to get the bare necessities. It is a fact in Canada today, I know in British Columbia, that children go to school hungry, and the Government says there is no money to feed them.
As I wind down my speech, I want to conclude by saying something I looked forward to saying since I was elected. I want to pay personal tribute to the Leader of our Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broad-bent), for the service he has rendered to this country.
I was disappointed when he said that he would step down. I had looked forward to serving in this Parliament under his leadership. Every day that he intervenes in the House I am renewed in the conviction that he has a tremendous place still to play in the history of this country. I believe our Party does him honour and I know this House does him honour.
I am gratefully looking forward to the opportunity of serving Victoria and my country as a Member of Parliament. It is a tremendous honour and one which I believe all Canadians should have the opportunity to experience. As one who has been chosen to exercise that responsibility, I can merely say that I will do my best in this position.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too should add my thoughts to those of the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. Brewin) about our Leader and the contribution he has made to this country and our Party in particular. There is still the future to hear from the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent).
April 11, 1989

I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Victoria and some of his close associates and friends on being awarded the Commonwealth Games for 1994 in Victoria. It will be a major event for his city and also one of which all of us from British Columbia are proud.
I would like him to comment on the question of our forests which, as I stated during the emergency debate on the massive oil spill off the coast of Alaska, is our greatest environmental heritage. I was pleased that the Hon. Member for Victoria at least mentioned forests in his speech, because we heard nothing about forestry in the Speech from the Throne.
Does he believe there is a train of thought on the government side-perhaps they are all empty cars-on the commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) time and time again about introducing legislation to create a full Department of Forests?
On January 30, he created the portfolio of Minister of State for Forests and said that legislation would follow. Would he comment on the regrettable statement by the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Oberle) who said that establishing a full Department of Forests is not a high priority of the Government.
Knowing the Member's concern about forestry and how it affects his riding, specifically Vancouver Island, does he see any concern about what impact that department may have on British Columbia and Vancouver Island?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one point the Government seemed to commit itself to the idea of having a full department of forestry. That was before the election. It seems to have vanished from its agenda now. This is a matter of great disappointment to the people of our area in particular.
Forestry is British Columbia's number one industry and is perhaps one of the major industries all across Canada. We are finally beginning to recognize the damage that we have done to our forests. Those who have worked in the forests, loggers and members of a number of the unions which I have been associated as legal counsel over a number of years, have for a long time seen what the problems were. They are caused primarily by a lack of management but also by a lack of government intervention to ensure management.
One of the problems is if the Government does not set down any rules, then each company is virtually forced to
The Address-Mr. Fontaine
do what it can get away with. Some companies have a slightly better record than others, but basically, all are driven by the bottom line, and it is their responsibility to their shareholders to try to extract as much as they can in the shortest possible time. This has left our forests denuded.
Even now, if one looks from Victoria toward Salt Spring Island, one can see that even the Gulf Islands are beginning to get caught. If one has an opportunity to fly across Vancouver Island, one will see that this is now becoming a major epidemic. This is happening in the interest of jobs now at the cost of jobs later.
It will be very important for all levels of government and the community to pull together to try to develop programs which will ensure that old growth forests such as the Carmanah Valley are preserved and at the same time ensure, to the fullest extent possible, that the first imperative is conservation.
The second imperative is, as far as possible, to get the maximum number of jobs out of our forests. This will include, for example, policies of prohibiting the export of raw logs and of ensuring the production of forest and lumber products here rather than abroad.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after every election campaign Canadians must expect a description of the Government's major policy orientations. We did that in 1984. After the victory of September 1984, we told Canadians we were going to create jobs, initiate economic renewal and enable Canadians to get jobs. This time again, we recently put forward and are discussing today our orientation for the next few years.
Firstly, Mr. Speaker, I would like to list and probably repeat the four major thrusts of our Throne Speech. First, to build a strong economy, encouraged by incentive and opportunity, an economy fully competitive among the world's trading nations and one in which all Canadians may share its challenges, risks and rewards.
Second, to strongly work out at preserving Canada's environment; to actively encourage increased public interest and involvement, and to give leadership and support to international efforts aimed at fighting the threats to this planet.

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Fontaine
Third, to maintain a caring, compassionate society which will be able, through continuing economic prosperity, to meet its obligations and responsibilities to those who are less fortunate and in greatest need.
Fourth, to foster a confident sense of Canada's cultural and national uniqueness.
Mr. Speaker, the first item in our message, and one I consider to be the key to the others is a strong economy. And today I am happy to take part in this statement on our strong economy. I notice that my colleague, the Hon. Member from Langelier (Mr. Loiselle), the Minister of State (Finances), is in the House. Since I am sure he played a part in drawing up this economic statement, whose objectives and philosophy I share, I wish to congratulate him for having mastered, in a few weeks, the complexities of the subject.
Mr. Speaker, a strong economy means getting rid of the public debt. Last year interest payments amounted to $1,300 for every man, woman and child in Canada. For the average family, this works out to $5,000 annually or $400 monthly. This represents a big chunk in our mortgage payments, in our salaries.
Today, Mr. Speaker, $31 out of every $100 collected by Revenue Canada go to pay the interest on old accounts, in many cases, on old grocery bills.
As long as we must spend such a disproportionate share of our total resources on interest payments, the economy will suffer.
To bring the point home, Mr. Speaker, we spend on interest payments twice the amount we spend on pensions and other benefits for senior citizens. We spend nearly 11 million dollars on national defence, yet we spend three times that amount on interest payments on old debts. We spend 20 times as much on interest charges as on job creation programs. We spend 24 times as much on interest as on our regional development programs.
Mr. Speaker, these expenditures must cease. We must get better control of our economy and free ourselves from these interest costs and to do so, we must reduce our deficit. How can we reduce this deficit? We have various possibilities; one of them, which will probably be put forward in the next budget speech, is tighter control of our Government's spending.
When we took power for the first time in 1984, the deficit in our expenditure programs as such, those on which we could decide, including interest costs, was
nearly $38 billion. We have progressively reduced it year by year to less than $30 billion. Since the budgets of 1987-88 and 1988-89, our expenditures are less than our revenues-and that is important-if interest charges are excluded. That means that if the Governments that preceded us had not run up such a large debt to keep power from one mandate to the next, we would not have to pay interest costs of over $30 billion today.
Of course, another way of controlling our deficit is to ask Canadians to participate more in what the Government is doing. The Minister of Finance will likely convince Canadians that everyone should pay for the mistakes of those who preceded us over the last 20 years. In the end, Canadians have to pay for the mistakes the Liberals made during all their terms in power, when they were in good economic times and continued to add to our country's debt. So all Canadians will have to tighten their belts some more.
Another way to reduce our deficit, and I am getting into specifics, is to modify our tax system as our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will probably do. Canada's tax system is lagging behind that of most European countries.
I suggest we gradually shift from income taxes to commodity taxes. We must also do away with certain taxes whose only effect is to thwart our economic development, and I have in mind the repeal of the 12 per cent tax on manufactured goods. This tax certainly does nothing to boost our exports because when we try to sell our products in the United States or elsewhere, they cost 12 per cent more. Another consequence of this tax is that it favours foreign imports to the detriment of our domestic producers, in the sense that the importer stands to benefit to the tune of 12 per cent on most of his imported goods because that tax does not apply to the products we buy from the United States or other countries.
The bottom line is that the Canadian manufacturer is the loser, too often to the benefit of his competitors elsewhere in the world. This levy brings in $15 billion a year to the Canadian Government, but it has to go.
Finally, another way to trim our deficit would be to gain better control over inflation so as to make our economy even more prosperous. Sure enough, a lot of people in the Opposition speak out against the official position of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his fight against inflation.
April 11, 1989

You know, Mr. Speaker, the easy way out would be to signal to the Canadian economy and the various interest groups that no attempt is to be made to control inflation. All we need do is print more money. In the short term this would relieve some of the pressure on rising interest rates because the more money is available, the more lenders lend and interest rates would have to come down.
Should that happen, within a short time-a few months-demand for goods and services of every description would increase because people would have more cash to spend. This higher demand could not be met by the supply, that is by people who make the goods and provide the services.
If you have a given quantity of goods in stock and people want more, you have two options: either you produce more or you raise prices to set a new demand level. With this kind of scenario we would soon find ourselves in a period of raging inflation which would be just as disastrous as what we experienced early in this decade. A policy to control and prevent inflation is therefore a means of controlling our deficit.
Finally, another system that will be put forward in a few months by our Minister of Finance, with whose goals and philosophy I could not agree more, is the value-added tax. That tax will bring the Government the equivalent of the revenue lost because of the lowering of other taxes. The value-added tax will bring the Government $23 billion when implemented, but those $23 billion will not bring one additional cent to the Government of Canada. They will replace $15 billion derived from the tax on manufactured goods. They will replace an estimated $3 billion lost because of tax reductions granted to some individuals.
And also that tax will replace another tax on certain personal tax benefits that were allowed under certain conditions, for a total $23 billion reduction in revenues derived from our present tax system in the areas of income tax and taxes on manufactured goods, in exchange of which the Government will collect $23 billion from the value-added tax. This will not be peculiar to Canada. It is a trend in the Western world. It is a trend in the free world and, for the benefit of my colleagues from the Socialist Party, let me tell them it will become-an income tax will probably be levied soon in the Soviet Union because they have decided among other things to understand and find it valuable to their economy to use certain principles of modern capitalism.
The Address-Mr. Fontaine
Finally, another solution to balance our budget and reduce the deficit and foster better economic renewal is the continuation of our privatization programs. You know that overall, Crown corporations still end up costing nearly $4 billion and a half to the Canadian taxpayers. Is it normal to ask every Canadian taxpayer to shoulder the unprofitability of certain Crown corporations in a context of economic difficulty? I do not think it is. Our government is sending out a clear signal. We will pursue our policy of privatization because, as Conservatives, we believe that the business community is better able to assess the appropriateness and profitability of an investment, to harness the human and material resources required to produce goods and services in Canada.
We maintain that bureaucrats cannot do this from their offices. Because we believe private enterprise is much more imaginative, much more in touch with reality, we intend to continue giving it greater responsibilities in the management of big corporations which were once owned by the Crown.
There is another major point. We all heard this morning the speech given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) on the new direction of unemployment insurance programs. Questions come to mind. Canadians from coast to coast often ask themselves about this or that individual who systematically misuses unemployment insurance. These abuses must stop. On the other hand, the Minister stated quite clearly that the government must continue to ensure the security of those who have lost their jobs through no fault of their own. But the government will question more and more the appropriateness of helping those who chronically misuse the system. We must put a stop to this abuse by any Canadian citizen from whatever region. Here again, we will set things straight while caring, as I have said, about those who really need unemployment insurance. On top of that, the Minister said that she would strive to help in the development of our human resources who, because of rapid technological changes, would not have been able to adjust to the lifestyle and jobs of today. Measures to help those people were announced this morning.
Another thing: as a Member of Parliament, I often receive in my riding office people who are entitled to 40 or 45 weeks worth of unemployment insurance benefits. They tell me that they are thinking of starting a small business with their brother-in-law, their friends, their old boss, their son or their daughter. So I went to the unemployment insurance office where I was told that, if I

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Fontaine
started a small business, I could no longer collect unemployment insurance because I would be unavailable for work. Well, the Minister solved that problem.
An important point made by our Minister of Employment and Immigration in her speech was that anyone eligible for benefits that can amount to $8,000, $10,000, $12,000 or $14,000 can now submit a business plan to the Employment Canada officer and if that plan is considered valid, Employment Canada will immediately give the applicant who wants to start a small business the benefits he or she would have received over 30, 40 or 50 weeks. It is another advantage. Under the old rules, the budding entrepreneur would have lost that money. Now he or she can keep it and may even become a reliable employer and Canadian producer of goods and services. That is cooperation with Canadians. It is a message that we Conservatives have trusted small, medium and big business. We give the unemployed who have difficulty starting a business the opportunity to become employers.
Mr. Speaker, another message. You know that Canadians attach great importance-and it is becoming a matter of life and death throughout the world-we must stress environmental protection more and more. And speaking of the environment, the Speech from the Throne says:
Protect the environmental integrity of our Arctic regions.
And that, Mr. Speaker, gives us a certain opening, for two reasons. These days, many use environmental reasons to criticize the plan to build nuclear-powered submarines. Everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that whenever a problem occurs in Canada, either someone is lost in a forest or on a hunting trip or a search mission or someone is lost at sea, the Canadian Forces are called on immediately. If the Canadian Forces had nuclear-powered submarines, instead of asking questions that today cannot be answered. .. Because recently, we saw Arctic mammals on television-and when I say mammals, I include humans-and it was observed that they were accumulating lead, PCBs and chemicals in their systems. At present, we have no way of controlling where that comes from. It is claimed that it might come from Arctic waters. But water in the Arctic is covered with ice twelve months a year. It should be realized the only way to check up on that is by way of submarines which we need, not only for military purposes but for the preventive and curative protection of our environment. The only means therefore is nuclear powered submarines.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, this can also have benefits for our economy, especially in the area where I live.
Finally, the Trone Speech refers to:
. . . initiatives to clean up the St. Lawrence River.
It is a major economic link between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic. The St. Lawrence will remain the major economic link between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic, but in addition it will become a river of drinking water and this is a matter to which we attach certain priorities.
Finally, our Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney's) position concerning an agreement with the United States on acid rain is stated again. We know that unfortunately we are very good importers of American acid rain, and we know that even if we clean up our own house, we still need an agreement with our neighbors to prevent their acidic emissions. This is part of the Throne Speech message.
A third element in the Throne Speech is the message concerning a caring nation. There are three groups of Canadians: the young, people in the workforce and I consider us here to be part of the working force, and those who were our predecessors in our society, the men and women who made it possible for us to be here today. They need us today, and our message points to the continuation of our generous plans for senior citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I would have more to say on our Throne Speech-I could comment on our co-operation in the search for better agreements with the GATT, but I wish to let other Members rise and have their say on the Throne Speech. In conclusion, I suggest that a favourable evolution of our economy is everyone's business. We must all take part-each one of us must do his or her share, because only in this way will we continue enjoying a better quality of life.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always listened with great pleasure to the Hon. Member for Levis who just gave us his views on the Speech from the Throne.
I must say I had trouble seeing nuclear attack submarines as beneficial to the ecology of my country. I found this rather hard to understand, and I am sure the Hon. Member would be willing to explain how an instrument of war could be beneficial to Canada's ecology, and more specifically, how the Hon. Member could possibly make such a statement, considering all the risks of having a vehicle, nuclear-powered or otherwise, in an environmentally sensitive area.
April 11, 1989

He also referred to the fact we would have to tighten our belts, saying we could not go on spending as if there was no tomorrow. I suggest we now have a good opportunity to save money by cancelling the whole nuclear submarine program which is going to cost Canadian taxpayers about $14 billion, even if they are ecological submarines according to my hon. friend opposite.
I have one last question, and perhaps he can answer all my questions at the same time. It's about this caring society. The Hon. Member referred to a caring society, and speaking as a Canadian, I think that in the past, we have had a society that I would call caring, at least compared to countries that do not have as many social programs as we do to help the needy.
Today, however, we heard the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) say in her speech that unemployment insurance recipients would see their benefits cut rather severely, even if they had very few prospects of finding a job elsewhere.
How can the Hon. Member claim his Government advocates this caring society, considering the statements that were made earlier today?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have been very disappointed if the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell had not asked me a few supplementaries today. We are starting another four-year term together, and I wish him the best of luck. And I hope that at the end of tips period, we will be able to renew our mandate together.
First of all, the Hon. Member mentioned the peacekeeping role and how it relates to the manufacturing of nuclear-powered submarines.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I was talking about the ecological role.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He mentioned the peace-keeping role and the ecological role. I will deal with each one separately.
Because of the improvers state of preparedness of our country and the quality of our military personnel that Canada has enjoyed such credibility over the past decades as a military force and has been called upon as much as 35 times, I believe, not to wage war, but to keep peace. And to be effective as a peace-keeping force, a country must be credible and well equipped. This goes to
The Address-Mr. Fontaine
show that peace-keeping and nuclear-powered submarines can go hand in hand.
Secondly, nuclear-powered submarines present no threat to the environment. They are no more dangerous than conventional submarines. As I have said, nuclear-powered submarines can, for days, weeks and months on end, travel under the polar ice cap conducting studies, taking water-quality samples, identifying sources of pollution which cannot be identified today because we cannot set up equipment there. And this is important because we see the effects of pollution on life in our northern regions.
Precisely because we attach so much importance to the protection of the environment, we need to go up there to see what is going on so as to avoid further accumulations of lead in Arctic life forms.
The Hon. Member wants to know how the Government can contemplate purchasing submarines at a cost of $14 billion. First of all, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is well aware that these submarines will cost exactly $8 billion, and not $14 billion. He is also aware that this cost will be spread over a 25 year period, which represents an average cost of $300 million a year, and that this purchase is necessary because it is recommended by the experts of our Armed Forces. Mr. Speaker, we certainly hope never to have to use these submarines in time of war, just like my fellow citizens and I hope never to need the services of the police. But when the mayor of our town decides to purchase a more modem car for our policemen, I say it is a good thing for these policemen to have the proprer equipment in case I should need it. And nobody blames the mayor for purchasing this upgraded equipment for our policemen, although we would prefer not to have to use it, but we know it is available. The same situation occurs on a national level. We need police cars to patrol our streets; we need more advanced equipment at the Provincial level, and we need still more sophisticated equipment at the Federal level.
In his last question, he referred to a generous economy. He wants to know on what this generous economy is based. When the Liberals were in power, the Government was most generous in incuring debts which we, our children and grand-children will have to pay back. That was how they redistributed the unearned wealth of the State, by accumulating debts which now amount to $320 billion. That is how generous that Government was!

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Fontaine
This Government, on the other hand, is being generous towards those men and women in our society who really need help; Mr. Speaker, we make it possible for our partners in the private sector to grow and make money. It is important to make money. We make it possible for them to make money. In turn, they will pay taxes, so that the Government will finally be able to share the earned wealth, instead of sharing debts which our children and grand-children who have no say about it, will have to pay back.
That is my understanding of a generous economy, Mr. Speaker.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congra-gulate you on your re-election. I think that the Edmonton North constituents made a good choice. I wish also to congratulate you for sitting in this House for the past 21 years. It is quite an achievement, and I hope that you will continue to seek the support of your constituents.
I certainly enjoyed the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), remarks which certainly reflect the policy of this Tory Government. Just the same, I should like to ask him a few questions, especially concerning Crown Corporations. He indicated that was one way we could bring down Canada's debt which now totals $320 billion.
Does the Hon. Member think that if we managed to privatize these corporations with a total value of some $13.5 billion, we could bring down Canada's debt while saving money, because we spend approximately $4 billion every year to operate them? That would make up a total of $17.5 billion. That is one of my questions.
I have a second question concerning the proposed value added tax. By the way, according to a study made in the United States, if that country wanted to institute a value added tax system, it would require approximately
21,000	employees more and cost $700 million to the US Treasury. In Canada, that would mean about 4,000 more civil servants, which would cost our Treasury, that is the Minister of Finance, something like $200 million, and all that, of course, in order to collect about $23 billion, as estimated by my friend, the Hon. Member for Levis.
I don't normally object to reducing the deficit. It certainly is a good idea. But I wonder if, by applying an added-value tax, we would not be creating another layer of bureaucracy in the Department of Finance. Consequently, shouldn't we look at this problem from another
perspective and try to find some other way to achieve a tax reform. For example, we could have a flat income tax rate of, let's say, 15 per cent. It would be simple enough and eliminate the need for more bureaucrats. Those are the two questions I wanted to ask the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the first question of the Hon. Member for Calgaiy-North-East (Mr. Kindy), I would like to show you the results that can be achieved by privatization and I will use, as an example, the Canada Post Corporation. When we were first elected, in 1984, that corporation was losing $381 million. Nowadays, thanks to the guidelines we, in the conservative government, established for the management of this corporation, it is no longer in the red. I use this example because this corporation is now working in cooperation with the private sector, has increased the accessibility and quality of its services to private companies, and has succeeded at no extra cost to Canadian taxpayers.
We also found out other advantages in privatization, in the case of Canadair, for instance, a company, with de Havilland, that swallowed $2.3 billion because of the carelessness of the Liberal administrators who set them up. We made them private companies. Canadair has now increased its personnel. It exports some of its products abroad, and all of them, Canadair, de Havilland and Canadian Arsenals are now profitable and have hired more employees although our privatization objectives had met with objections. The Socialists and Liberals said at the time it was nonsense and that every one of the workers would lose his job. Quite the contrary! Nobody lost his job. Canadians have better jobs and more of them are working.
As for my colleague's concerns regarding the cost of collecting the added-value tax, I must inform him it is a matter that surely worries my colleague from Langelier who is Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Loiselle). I must also point out to him that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is working in co-operation with the representatives of the Finance Ministers of the ten Canadian provinces in an attempt to institutionalize a collection system that will take into account past experiments of previous systems, for example, the collection of tax on manufactured goods. Hopefully, there will be a very close and formal co-operation among provinces. Thus, we expect to reduce to a minimum the collection costs of the added-value tax.
April 11, 1989

The Address-Mr. Walker

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the hon. gentleman for taking part in the Throne Speech debate. However, I am sure he would want his copy of Hansard to set the record straight.
He grouped Canadians into three categories-the young, the active and the elderly, as if to imply that the elderly are not active.
On Saturday I delivered an Horizons cheque to a Mrs. Rae in my riding. She is 83 years old and no relation to the leader of the provincial NDP. She lives in an apartment complex in which the seniors have very little to do. Yet, at the age of 83, suffering from arthritis and walking with the use of a cane, she took on a project of setting up a program for senior citizens in two apartment buildings. She is more active than the young people the Hon. Member put in his active category. I think we should set the record straight in this House. Many of the elderly are just as active, and in fact maybe more active, than some of our young Canadians.
I wanted to pose a question to the Hon. Member. I am pleased that he did address the deficit problem, but I wonder if he would set the record straight. I am sure it will look nice in his Hansard when he sends it out to his constituents. What was the public debt when his Party took office in 1984, and what is the public debt today. Could he explain why in the best of economic times, from 1984 to 1989, at a time when Canada never experienced such good economic times before, at a time when his Government sold off many Crown corporations creating billions of dollars as revenue for the Government, why has his Government allowed the public debt to rise to such an extent?
I think his colleague in his question said the public debt is something like $320 billion. So I wonder if he could tell this House exactly what was the accumulated public debt in 1984, what is it today and why his Government allowed it to grow that much?
He blames governments over the last 20 years. Past Governments went through good times, but they also had recessions. They built in a lot of new programs, but here is a Government in the best of economic times boasting to Canadians how they are reducing the deficit while hiding under the mat what is happening to the public debt. This is the real issue here. Let us be honest with Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to give short answers to the two questions of the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis).
In his first question he asked me to define what I understand by the young, the active, and the elderly. When I say active, Mr. Speaker, I refer to the group of people defined by Statistics Canada as being the men and women who, usually between the ages of 20 and 60 or 65, are considered in the labour force. That is the word economists and stastisticians use to refer to gainfully employed people.
As to the second question concerning the trend of the deficit between 1984 and 1988,1 am very pleased to have this opportunity to explain why our deficit now stands at $320 billion. Why do Canadians have to pay so much for the deficit? Because for years on end-from the time the present Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) was Minister of Finance-the Liberal Government systematically conducted its election campaigns on the strength of very expensive and very costly promises, and it had to pile up a series of deficits. So now we are paying interests on those loans.
When we took over in 1984 the economy was in such bad shape that we could not overdo it in terms of cutting expenditures and raising taxes. First we had to set the economy on an even keel. We did that, but we had no choice but continue to pay interests on the debts of our Liberal predecessors, and pay interests we did. Gentlemen, we had to service your debt and this is why we had to live with a soaring over-all debt in this country. Today, because of the irresponsibility of your colleagues and of your present leader, who was Minister of Finance when the deficits began to pile up. . . It is because of your irresponsibility that Canada has now accumulated a deficit of $320 billion.
