Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. A Speech from the Throne is normally a time for a government to signal its concern about the state of the country, to outline the solutions that government intends to follow. All parliamentarians are concerned about the financial mess this Government has created, and we can understand this Government's preoccupation, if not downright panic, caused by the incompetence of its Ministers.

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Walker
We also find it incomprehensible that the needs of so many Canadians are not even mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. It is not that those in need expect big chunks of money; they know that these are saved for Club Ritz Carleton, but think of the following: There is no mention of the homeless in this speech. Perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has changed his mind since the election when he said that one homeless person in Canada is too many. Maybe he now agrees with his former Minister of Housing who said that the homeless people do not want permanent homes.
The good intentions of the present housing Minister can do nothing to help those who are living under bridges or who are sleeping in doorways if the Prime Minister will not follow through on his commitment. Money has been spent by this Government to study this problem, but where is the money to solve it? It is certainly not on the streets of Winnipeg.
Also, Mr. Speaker, there has been no mention of the post-secondary education needs of native youth. Yet this Government is content to restrict access to education while saying they are prepared to give more money. They are saying you can go to school, you can get an education, but it has to be on our terms and you have to go where we tell you to go and study what we want you to study.
Even the Minister responsible for this mess follows this line. Those students felt they had no other means of protest other than going on a hunger strike, Mr. Speaker. If you want to talk to the Minister, you have to see him only under his normal conditions. I am not satisfied about this policy, and neither are the native communities across Canada. This is one of the most scandalous changes in the federal attitude toward aboriginal peoples, and this Government is going to let a generation of native students, whose only goal is to better themselves, pay the price.

Mr. Speaker, there is a lot of poverty in the city of Winnipeg and more specifically in my riding, especially among the elderly. According to official figures, 5,000 people in this group have an annual income of $7,000 or less. There is nothing for the elderly in the Speech from the Throne. I say we need programs and agreements for agriculture, science and transport, and so forth. What will my city's future be under a Conservative Government?

Mr. Speaker, I begin my comments on the Speech from the Throne by first congratulating you, Mr. Speaker, for your re-election to the House and for your appointment as our Deputy Chairman of the Committee of the Whole.
In commenting on the Speech from the Throne, I would like to begin with an economic theme and place it within the context of where we have been and what has been achieved over the past four years, as well as where we are heading now as indicated by the Speech from the Throne.
Since September, 1984, 1,432,000 jobs have been created. To put it another way, from 1984 through to 1988, more jobs were created in Canada than in all of the
following countries combined: West Germany, France, Sweden, Belgium, Greece, Finland, Ireland, New Zealand, and Australia.
The national unemployment rate has fallen from 11.6 per cent to 7.5 per cent. In total, Canada's economy has expanded by 19 per cent. In real terms, after taking into account inflation, the economy has expanded by 19 per cent since September, 1984. Business investment in new machinery and equipment has climbed by 76 per cent since 1984. New orders in manufacturing have climbed by 33 per cent. Some 223,000 homes were built in 1988 compared to 135,000 in 1984, the year we were elected to our first mandate.
The number of Canadians living below the poverty line has fallen by 549,000 since 1984. Not only is that figure remarkable and important, but it includes 179,000 fewer children and 61,000 fewer senior citizens. In looking at the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, it will do much to improve our economic performance.
The Finance Department study concluded that the agreement should lead to the creation of 120,000 net new jobs, while the Economic Council study forecasts
250,000	net new jobs by 1998 over the 10-year phasing-in period of this agreement. With the victory of the Conservative Government, new investment has increased dramatically in my riding and in the cities surrounding my riding of Kitchener-Waterloo, Cambridge and Guelph in southwestern Ontario.
When I look at the question of investment, total capital spending by business is expected to climb by 11 per cent this year, including a 21 per cent increase in manufacturing investment. In the 12 months following the negotiation of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, the annual rate of investment in new machinery and equipment climbed by 17 per cent in real terms, after taking inflation into account. To put this in perspective, 17 per cent in one year exceeds the total growth of 12 per cent that occurred in the four and a half years between 1980 and 1984 when the Liberals were in power. The annual number of small business births has climbed by 35 per cent since 1984.
Inflow of direct foreign investment doubled between 1984 and 1988. In my riding and the neighbouring ridings around me, it is difficult to find labourers for construction work to complete many of these construction projects.
April 11, 1989

Of these 1,432,000 jobs that have been created since September of 1984, including 86,000 in the first three months of this year, 85 per cent of those jobs have been full time. In contrast, 89 per cent of the jobs created by the last Liberal administration were part time.
When I refer to the number of jobs created during the term of this Government, I do not want to suggest that this Government created those jobs. Governments do not create jobs; people create jobs.
What Governments do is create a climate for investment and initiative where people take it upon themselves to create jobs, or Governments bring in policies that reduce that initiative, frighten off new investment and lessen the ability of individuals to create jobs. I am simply stating figures during the time of an administration.
Let us look at job creation as it affects women in our society. Some 807,000 more women are working today than in September, 1984. The unemployment rate for women has fallen by four percentage points since the election, from 11.9 to 7.9.
In comparison, the rate increased by 3.3 points under the last Liberal administration, from 8.6 to 11.9. Perhaps more significant, between 1984 and 1988, the number of women working in managerial and administrative positions climbed by 50 per cent. Managerial and administrative positions accounted for one-quarter of the jobs created for women between 1984 and 1988. Including occupations such as teaching, medicine and law, almost half the jobs created for women between 1984 and 1988 were of a managerial, administrative or professional nature.
If we look at youth unemployment figures from 1984 through to today, that rate has fallen from 18.2 per cent in September of 1984 to 10.6 per cent, its lowest level in 14 years. I was struck by an article in the Kitchener-Water-loo Record entitled "Students to enjoy a boom in summer jobs". The writer of the article had gone to post-secondary institutions in the neighbouring riding of Waterloo. In talking to people at the universities, he found the following:
Jan Basso, the director of career services at Wilfrid Laurier University, estimates summer-job availability is up by as much as 10 per cent in 1988.
In addition, Basso said salaries seem to be higher, with many more jobs in the $7-to-$8-an-hour range.
"There are lots and lots of (summer) jobs out there", added Kerry Mahoney, assistant supervisor of the University of Waterloo's career
The Address-Mr. Reimer
resources centre. 'Any student wanting a summer job this year should be able to get one. Many students can be quite particular, especially if they do their research and if they started early."
The increase in the availability of career-related jobs is particularly promising. Sharon Keogh, Conestoga College's career and placement services manager, said jobs range from general labour and clerical to career-related types in everything from construction to computers and accounting.
Thanks to a strong economy, placement officers with postsecondary institutions say the summer of '89 promises to be a veiy good year indeed. They say it's going to be even better than 1988, which was considered an exceptionally good year.
A major theme in the Speech from the Throne was the need for deficit reduction. The last Liberal Government, when it was in power from 1980 to 1984, increased spending by an average annual rate of 15.1 per cent. Under this administration, from 1984 to 1988, that increase in spending of 15.1 per cent was reduced to an average of 4.3 per cent, or about equal to inflation. If this Government had continued in 1984 at the Liberal rate of spending, the deficit would not have been reduced from
38.3	down to 28.9, as we expect for this year, but the annual deficit for this year would be about $58 billion higher or approximately $87 billion this year.
We can see what has been achieved and where we have come from. When we took office in 1984, the Liberal Government was spending approximately $16 billion more than it was taking in through taxation. This administration significantly reduced that excessive spending in its first year from $16 billion down to $9 billion, to $3 billion, to $1 billion, and in the past year to $4 billion.
Although we have taken positive action in reducing the amount we are spending compared to the amount we are taking in, it is not good enough because we are constantly adding to the debt. We are adding to the interest we have to pay on that debt. It is a good start, but it is not good enough because we are still adding to the problem. That is why it is essential that government spending is cut, that we increase taxes, and that we continue to promote an expanding economy to create new wealth and tax dollars to help us to address that problem. We can then reduce the annual deficit to the point where we are creating a surplus and can finally begin to attack the national debt to which we keep adding every year. The Speech from the Throne highlighted this issue in sharp focus. It stated that 31 cents out of every dollar that comes into the federal treasury goes to pay interest on the debt. If action is not taken, that will escalate and climb.

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Reimer
Another major theme in the Speech from the Throne was the topic of the environment. Over the last decade it has become very clear that the world is facing an environmental challenge of unprecedented magnitude. It is not productive to sit around and blame one another. It is time for action. If any topic deserves non-partisan treatment, it is this one. We are all to blame, and we must all take action.
During the election the environment emerged as one of the primary issues. Of course, free trade was the prime issue, but the environment was second. In my riding, if the questions were not about free trade, they were about the environment.
The opposition Parties dismissed the record of the Government, but it has proved its commitment to the environment with action and not mere words. In the Speech from the Throne the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) made a commitment to include the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) as part of the strategic planning and priorities cabinet committee.
Let us review the performance of the Government, where we have come from and where we are heading on this issue. To combat acid rain, the Government passed the toughest car and truck emission control standards in the world. During the last mandate the Prime Minister was able to obtain a commitment from the former President of the United States. It was the first commitment to American-shared responsibility for the problem of acid rain, and also a pledge to spend $2.5 billion to fight acid rain. We are all encouraged by the new administration under President George Bush, and also by initiatives taken in Congress that show a willingness to go further and begin to attack the problem of acid rain. Agreements have also been signed between the federal Government and the provinces to cut acid rain emissions in half by 1994.
Canada also initiated and gained the first worldwide agreement to protect the ozone layer at an international conference held in Montreal in 1987. In 1988, the Government passed the Canadian Environmental Protection Act to ensure that Canadians have a right to a healthy environment.
In the Speech from the Throne we see it is our goal to develop policies that reflect the concept of sustainable development. "Sustainable development" are two very important words which came to us from the United Nations commission which looked at the question of
environment and development. I was struck by the words of Prime Minister Brundtland of Norway whose landmark report on environment and development was produced at the United Nations. She had the following to say about Canada and the environment:
Canada was one of the commission's midwives, one of its strongest political supporters. Few other countries have contributed so greatly to the report as Canada. . .and Canada reacted most strongly and positively to our report, not least by establishing the task force on environment and economy, a unique body in modem policymaking.
The international community is looking at this issue very seriously and when commenting on Canada has stated that a good start has been made.
In the Speech from the Throne there are other initiatives. For example, in Winnipeg there will be the creation of a centre for international promotion of sustainable development. We will hear more about the round table on environment and the economy, chaired by the President of McGill University. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) has been given new responsibilities to ensure that environmental issues are fully considered in the course of all government decision-making.
Environmental protection is not only the job of governments. It is the responsibility of each and every one of us. That is why the Speech from the Throne also stated that we want to encourage individual Canadians to become more aware of the environment with the establishment of an environmental partners' fund, the promotion of environmentally friendly products, and programs to encourage recycling.
I was encouraged by another theme in the Speech from the Throne regarding policies to strengthen the family unit. For too long the family has been neglected by government. I applaud the Prime Minister for his emphasis on the family unit, Canada's basic social institution. After all, the family unit is a fundamental building block of society.
The Government has and will continue to take important steps to curb the abusive influence of drugs upon society. The Prime Minister was truly visionary in his past assessment that drugs were approaching an epidemic level. Therefore, through government initiatives, a commitment was made to spend $210 million on a five-year ongoing program involving five different ministries to fight drug abuse. Without his leadership and the initiatives which he began, Canada would undoubtedly be fighting a battle of even greater magnitude.
April 11, 1989

I was struck by a small booklet on Canada's youth entitled "Ready For Tomorrow". It was commissioned by the Minister of State for Youth and Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Charest). It is a very good attitudinal study on young people aged 15 to 24. In this age group the young people value certain things as being very important. Although the family was not at the top of the list, it still received a strong two-thirds recognition of being very important in their lives. That is significant.
Those young people are very optimistic about future prospects for traditional marriage and of the family unit as we have always understood it. Some 69 per cent think it is very likely that they will stay married; an additional 29 per cent think it fairly likely they will keep that commitment to the same person for life. Only four in
1,000	think it is likely that they will experience separation and divorce. We would all welcome that statistic.
We should encourage Government and all departments, specifically the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty), the Minister of State for Youth and Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Jelinek) to ensure that all policy decisions taken will help these young people and others, and will help the family unit and contribute to strengthening that unit within our society. I am also encouraged by what the Government has planned to assist in strengthening the family.
I am disappointed that the plague of pornography was not mentioned in the Throne Speech. As a caring and compassionate nation, we must be committed to the eradication of this harmful material. Pornography, like drugs, affects all Canadians, especially youth. Like drug abuse which begins with softer drugs and leads to harder and more damaging drugs, pornography begins at a softer level and progresses to a hard-core level. Extensive research indicates, beyond any reasonable doubt, that pornography is addictive, pornography desensitizes, and if allowed to escalate, hard-core pornography can lead to harmful acting out of that which is portrayed. I strongly urge the Government to bring back one of the two Bills introduced in the last term and that we deal with this question.
Mr. Speaker, you have signalled that I have but one minute left in my allotted time. I am encouraged that the
The Address-Mr. Reimer
Government will deal with the very difficult and divisive question of abortion. We know it is a difficult question. I am encouraged that it will deal with it. I am prepared to face the responsibility of doing so.
I urge that we as Members of Parliament set an example to the nation and that we all remember something. Let us remember where we are. Let us remember who we are. Let us remember the trust that has been placed in us. Let us govern our behaviour accordingly so that when the country views us in action here, its respect for this federal institution will increase, as well as its respect for Members of Parliament. I may be a bit too optimistic and a bit naive but I still think it is a very high calling to serve one's fellow man in public office. I think it is time for us to all unite together to make sure that when people look at us they say: "That is true, and I would like to do that some day too".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was impressed with the comments of the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) and how committed he is to the neo-Tory agenda. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said today that he really did not make any campaign promises, he only made spending commitments. If they are spending commitments then they were made before the election was called. That sounds as if none of those commitments can be broken. But to listen to the Hon. Member for Kitchener, it sounds as if he would like to break as many of those commitments as possible and consider them as promises. I would be interested to know which of the spending commitments catalogued in The Globe and Mail of April 10 he would like to see broken so that he can implement the agenda which he seems to have been spelling out in his speech.
For instance, there is the Hibernia oil field development and $1 billion for the OSLO oil sands project in northern Alberta. There is $800 million over 15 years for the Newfoundland Railroad. There is $515 million over five years for regional development in Quebec. There is $420 million for all-terrain vehicles for the Canadian Forces, as well as $400 million in new equity for the Farm Credit Corporation. There is $400 million for the federal share of the Husky Oil upgrader in Lloydminster, $250 million over five years for the Canadian film industry and $1 billion in additional support for farmers. Since we are debating an amendment which I put relating to farmers, I would be interested to know what the Hon. Member's position is on that one.

April 11, 1989
The Address-Mr. Reimer
There is $150 million for construction of a natural gas pipeline to Vancouver Island, $129 million over five years for AIDS research, $110 million for the clean-up of the St. Lawrence River, $110 million for the national campaign against illiteracy and $88 million for support and adjustment for the grape and wine industry in Ontario and Quebec as a result of the free trade deal. Of course, there is an $8 billion price tag for the new nuclear submarine program.
Obviously, the Hon. Member for Kitchener is very determined that the Government should not keep these commitments, as outlined in his speech. I wonder which ones he thinks the Government should break. It seems evident that the Government in its Budget on April 27 is planning to break some of these, not promises but commitments that were made before the election was called last November.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) I would like to say that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has an excellent record, if we consider his Budgets over the past four years. At those times he brought with him his figures and his spending projections and just where the deficit will be at the end of that time. If I am not mistaken, three out of the four times he was below what he projected and did better than he thought he could do. The other time I believe he was just slightly over. That is a far cry from what we used to see between 1980 and 1984.
I think that if the Hon. Member were to read the whole article he would have noticed that the Minister of Finance indicated that those commitments were made, and that they were called commitments as opposed to promises because each one was budgeted for. Each one was in a Budget of the federal Government. Therefore, he knew that the spending and the requirement for funding was there and accounted for. If the Minister of Finance were here he would echo what I am saying right now. He would say that we have already planned for those expenditures and that they are in the Budget. That is why they are a commitment.
We all know that the Minister of Finance, on behalf of us all, has to deal with the fact of the deficit. He has to deal with the fact that 31 cents out of every dollar taken in goes to pay interest on the debt. We have to reduce that. I am sure my hon. friend wants to join us in reducing that.
I will not exercise my privilege to go on and say where a lot of that debt came from. The Hon. Member knows where it came from. Let us leave it at that. These are commitments that are in the Budget as distinct from
promises made by someone else on top of everything else the Government is going to do.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) began his remarks by addressing the Free Trade Agreement. That is one of the reasons I am here. The constituents of Parkdale- High Park voiced a very strong objection to the Free Trade Agreement in its format and its lack of protection for companies which might be affected by it. I am sure that as recently as last weekend the Hon. Member read in many newspapers about a number of companies that manufacture auto parts which are now moving to Mexico where the labour is 55 cents an hour, $5 a day. How is his Government going to address this issue? It is just the tip of the iceberg. There will be hundreds of similar companies moving to Mexico and other countries, or even to the United States where labour is cheaper. Does this mean that we in Canada have to lower our minimum wage? Does it mean we have to lower our pension plan for workers? Does it mean we have to lower our job safety record? Has this Government looked at some way of preserving the jobs of Canadians working in these factories, who are going to be unemployed because the companies are moving to Mexico where the labour is 55 cents a day?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) is correct in saying that in the past election the Free Trade Agreement was a major issue. I have a great many auto parts suppliers in and around my riding. In fact, if I were to take five of the ridings together around there I would see there are well over 15,000 people who work directly in that market and about another 17,000 who service those people. Of course, there are many others involved. There are over
30,000	people involved either directly or indirectly in the auto parts industry who are benefiting from the fact that those people are very busy and working. It is a very important topic.
In response to the point he has made, I would like to read to him a letter from one of the largest auto parts producers in my riding, Bud Automotive. Let me just read what the President and General Manager of Bud Automotive stated with regard to the Free Trade Agreement in auto parts. He said: "Free trade in the auto industry has been good for Canada and Ontario. But Canada would probably not exist were it not for free trade. The Free Trade Agreement with the United States opens up new enlarged market opportunities for Canadian industries." That is what people directly involved in the auto parts industry are saying. It is one of the largest employers in my riding.
April 11, 1989

In that context I say to the Hon. Member that Members opposite are always raising the prospect of some fear that a plant might close down here or there. That is the difference between the two sides in this House in this debate. Instead of always looking for an example of one little change, this side of the House says: "Look at all the opportunities that are coming. Look at the new potential that is there". That is the difference. I am sorry it has to be such a sharp difference. Surely, everyone can see that if we secure trade with our largest trading partner and we bring in some rules to govern that trading arrangement and we enlarge the opportunity to trade further within that agreement, then the net result is gain. And there is no question of that. If it were true that everyone was going to move to where it is $4 or $5 an hour or even less, then why have they all not started to move? Why is there not a mass exodus out of the northeastern United States to the southern States, from the southern States into Mexico, et cetera?
Maybe my hon. friend can point to a few examples, but surely the industry itself says that it is going to be good for us, and so I will take their word for it. Thank you.

I have a response to the two-part question. For the first part, those figures simply come from the Library here. They are StatsCan figures. Those figures are not debatable figures. Facts are facts, whether you like them or not. You can find those same facts and you can use them any way you wish.
With regard to the plight of the homeless, it is true we have food banks in some of our cities and it is true that even in some of the most affluent areas of our cities and ridings across the country, we have some school children who do not go to school with a proper breakfast.
Mr. Speaker, I would respond that the best social policy then is a job. This Government has got a very good record in encouraging job creation, and the Free Trade Agreement is one part of that strategy. We have to look forward to increasing trade with the Pacific Rim, to increasing our trade with Europe. Let us look at what is going to take place in Europe in 1992, continue to increase jobs and therefore the wealth of this country, to help those in need and create opportunities for full-time jobs.
The second part of the question had to do with abortion. The Government has simply said it is prepared to bring this issue forward. It is a free vote issue on this side of the House. I am not sure what the other Parties will do.
I do not know how many of my colleagues have read the Law Reform Commission Report called the Protection of Life, Crimes Against the Fetus. In the minority report section of that there is a very good statement by Commissioner Maingot which I would like to quote: "The criminal law is our nation's fundamental statement of public policy. It is the instrument by which the community draws a line between the tolerable and intolerable. Criminal law defines those whose interests are worthy of respect and protection, and in my view this should include all members of the human family. Ultimately the criminal law is a mirror of what we are. It reflects our commitment or lack of commitment to human dignity and equality".

I hope that when others contribute to this debate, they will realize that whatever we end up doing, that will reflect our collective commitment or lack of commitment to human dignity and to equality. subtopic: AGRICULTURE-PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION FOR DROUGHT-RELEASE OF DATA
AGRICULTURE-PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION FOR DROUGHT-RELEASE OF DATA
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. On April 4, the first day that this House returned, I stood in my place to ask a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) and got a response from the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer). I was seeking information about the Government's drought program. To this date there has probably not been a farm program in any country that has stirred up more questions nor been waiting longer for answers. In the Question Period we elicited only minimal information from the Minister. He told us, and I quote from page 37 of Hansard:
The information regarding crop losses and the basis for the maps that were established, the information was based on a loss to coverage ratio through crop insurance records which was exactly the procedure that was used in 1985 that people did not like.
I wanted to put that on the record, Mr. Speaker, because the immediate question is: if people did not like it in 1985, why in heaven's name did the Government perpetuate the same idiotic system on the farmers in the drought of 1988?
He went on to tell us that the final data is not in yet. He tried to tell us that the program was designed by farmers, it is they who wanted us to target it, they wanted us to be crop specific, they wanted to get down to the smallest possible area, this is exactly what in fact we are doing. I take issue with that, Mr. Speaker.
It is quite clear that there was a better way of doing this. The NDP and myself put forward a program for the election last fall to put pressure on the Government to adopt a more sane policy of making drought payments. We had suggested that they use crop insurance data, and the smallest possible unit that it is possible to pay out under crop insurance is on an individual farm basis, farm by farm.
Instead of accepting that rational approach, the Government has once again insisted upon paying on a township by township basis so that each of the farmers who have land in each township will get a different factor of payment for each crop. This tends to be unfair and unequal and, even worse, creates an unnecessary production of data that nobody bothers to generate except on the instruction of the Government for a crop drought payment.
Now, the program that we suggested would have used data that is generated because it has to be by crop insurance, and yet the Government refused to use that data. They could have had the payments in the hands of those farmers who had crop insurance contracts almost immediately.
Most of those farmers had to be investigated and have their claim justified. The amount of loss would be known to the files in crop insurance. The Government rejected that simple and helpful suggestion, to go on and use the system that it is perpetuating on farmers once again. I want to reiterate that it is a system that the Minister himself says: "which was exactly the procedure that we used in 1985, and I stress that people did not like".
I have great difficulty understanding a Government that has this kind of feedback and persists in perpetuating a program that no one liked the last time it was used, and persists in putting it forward again.
April 11, 1989

It is failing to provide real numbers to people so that they can understand how the program will work. It has been a complete disaster. Although it has been before the public for six months, no one really knows how the program works to this very day.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION FOR DROUGHT-RELEASE OF DATA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to provide details on the effective efforts by this Government to deliver the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program to Canadian farmers.
The Drought Assistance Program is helping producers who were hurt by the 1988 drought. The Government is making every effort to deliver a program that treats producers in many different circumstances fairly.
We anticipate that about 120,000 producers may qualify for drought assistance, with over 100 different crops in over 4,500 townships. It takes time to develop and deliver a program that deals with so many producers in so many types of circumstances.
On March 3, maps showing preliminary drought zones were issued. The information on these maps is based on preliminary crop insurance data supplied by provincial crop insurance agencies. The administration used this data to define preliminary drought zones so that interim payments could be made to farmers in the hardest hit areas.
These areas are not final. We will be able to announce the final drought areas when all crop insurance data is in.
The Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program administration is working hard to deliver this program to Canadian farmers. More than 145 people are directly involved in the delivery of the program, including the people on the toll-free line who have been answering up to 4,000 calls a week.
Recently, in response to the number of telephone calls, we doubled the number of operators on the toll-free line to 20.
The administration is putting interim payments into the hands of producers as quickly as possible. About 4,500 townships have been designated as drought areas on the basis of preliminary provincial crop insurance data. More drought areas may be designated when final data is available from provincial crop insurance agencies. That will probably take place by May.
Adjournment Debate
Personalized applications have been mailed to about
120.000	producers in designated drought areas and about
90.000	forms have been returned to date.
I am pleased to inform the House that interim cheques to producers began being mailed the week of March 27. Most should be in the hands of producers by spring seeding.
About 65,000 producers will get interim payments. The payments will average about $4,300 and will total about $280 million. The timing of these interim payments is similar to the timing of interim payments under last year's Special Canadian Grains Program.
Final payments are scheduled to be mailed in July. We are making progress on other aspects of the program as well.
A method for delivering assistance to Ontario horticultural producers has been established. We are working with horticultural groups in other provinces to establish a method of making payments.
Progress is being made in talks with the Province of Quebec on a proposal for program delivery. Discussions are continuing with the provinces on cost sharing. In addition, I can tell the House that producer review committees will be established in each province.
This program may be rather complex but it is resulting in individual tailoring of payments and an accurate assessment of each producer's needs.
The Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program is fair, well targeted, and timely. It is being delivered effectively by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, last week on April 4, 1989, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to intervene in the tragic case of Mr. Georgy Samoilovich of Moscow, a refusnik who is dying of cancer. I met his wife in Moscow on March 30, 1989.
This former mathematician first applied to leave the Soviet Union with his wife and son in 1972. He was continually refused an exit visa on the contention that he possessed secrets.
Even General Secretary Gorbachev has stated that the possession of secrecy rule should not apply for more than five years. The Samoilovich family has suffered hardship and deprivation for 17 years simply because it wanted to exercise a fundamental human right, the right to leave their country.
I brought up the Samoilovich case with two Soviet officials in Moscow on Thursday, March 30. They were

April 11, 1989
Adjournment Debate
very familiar with this case, and I got the distinct impression that they really had no justifiable reason to deny further Mr. Samoilovich an exit visa, especially when he is so much in need of medical treatment for enlarged lymph glands. This treatment has been offered at the Royal Marsden Hospital in London, England, through the British Embassy in Moscow.
Fortunately, the Samoilovichs were advised on April 5 that he would be allowed to go to London for medical treatment. We are very grateful for this news. We hope it is not too late.
I have been chairman of the Canadian Parliamentary Group for Soviet Jewry since December, 1986.
There is no question that dramatic changes have occurred in the Soviet Union over the past two years. Since General Secretary Gorbachev announced their new policies of glasnost and perestroika, Mr. Gorbachev has both pleased and shocked the world over various announcements of change, particularly those connected with arms reductions and other major decisions such as the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan.
There have also been significant changes in the number of Soviet Jews who have been granted exit visas. In 1982, only 2,688 refusniks were granted exist visas. In 1986, the number dropped to 914. Then surprisingly, the number of refusniks receiving an exist visa increased sharply to 8,155 in 1987 and then more than doubled to 18,965 in 1988.
My previous visit to the Soviet Union was in May, 1987.1 led a delegation from the Canadian Parliamentary Group for Soviet Jewry. We met with such high profile refusniks as Ida Nudel and Vladimir Slepak. I also met with members of the refusnik family which I had adopted, the Shnirman family.
Most of these people were released just months after our visit. It was thrilling to see many of these refusniks at the human rights rally sponsored by the North American Jewish Community in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, December 5, 1987. This was on the eve of General Secretary Gorbachev's visit to the U.S. and his meeting with President Reagan. I had the honour to represent Canada at this historic rally and to address over 200,000 people.
As mentioned earlier, many remarkable and progressive initiatives have been announced by the Soviet Union. While most countries in the western world applaud these initiatives, we must harbour some doubt and scepticism when it still takes years for a person dying of cancer to obtain an exit visa.
The Soviet Union wants to host an international human rights conference in Moscow in 1990 or 1991. Before Canada and other nations totally embrace and support this idea, I believe the Soviet Union should be confronted with the facts about many refusniks who are still struggling without success to leave the Soviet Union, and other human rights violations.
On March 29 and on March 30, 1989, I met with several of these desperate, discouraged refusniks in Moscow. I would like to highlight the facts concerning several of these people who simply dream and yearn to live in another country.
Igor Uspensky and his wife first applied to leave the Soviet Union in 1979. They were refused on the basis that Inna's brother, Professor Alexander Ioffe, had worked with classified material 10 years previously. Both Uspensky's were entomologists. In December, 1981, Inna was expelled from the institute and one year later Igor was dismissed. He has worked as a lift operator to avoid being persecuted as a "parasite".
On March 30,1 also met with Boris Chernobilsky and his wife Elana along with several other refusniks at their apartment. Mr. Chernobilsky first applied for an exit visa in 1976, 13 years ago.
The latest reason for refusing to grant an exit visa, according to the Soviet authorities, is the lack of a waiver. Boris' mother-in-law will not sign a waiver form which parents and in-laws have been required to sign in recent years.
When I discussed this rule with Soviet officials, and the fact that these in-laws or parents had absolute veto, I pressed the point about why this could not be changed. He mentioned that new laws which will be passed in six to twelve months could very well include a review of that, so there would be an appeal procedure.
The Roitman family of Kishinev was also discussed. They are also being denied an exit visa because Izik's father refuses to sign the waiver form.
There is some good news as well. I was, for instance, led to believe that the Livshitz family may finally receive their exit visa after languishing in despair for 10 years since applying in 1979. They received the good news last week. Similarly, I also got the distinct impression that Soviet authorities may finally reconsider their previous decisions of constant denials of exit visas to the Lurie family.
In closing, I want to commend General Secretary Gorbachev for many of the progressive initiatives put forth, particularly over the past two years. However,
April 11, 1989

there are still many Soviet citizens being denied the simple human right to leave their country. With the stroke of a pen, certain restrictive regulations could be changed. With the stoke of a pen, every one of the these long-standing refusniks could be granted an exit visa.
I urge the Soviet Union to stop using these unfortunate souls as hostages. Let them leave. Let them live. Grant them this basic human right. Only then will the Soviet Union have earned the right to host an international human rights conference.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Markam (Mr. Attewell) for raising the specific case he has and for raising the question of the general policy.
On the same date last week as the Hon. Member for Markam asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) whether he would intervene in order to support Mr. Samoilovich's application for an exit visa to go to London, Mr. Samoilovich was in fact granted permission to leave. I understand that the editors of the Guinness Book of World Records are still debating now whether to grant an award to the Hon. Member for Markam for his acuity and timing or to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his alacrity in response.
The fact is, of course, that this was just one of a number of cases that has currently been raised by our Government in order to see, under the Helsinki Accord's family reunification provisions, that those seeking freedom in the West are able to obtain permission to come to the West. Certainly the granting of this permission to leave was welcome news.

Mr. Speaker, I hope we will see even fewer cases as the Soviet Union implements the provisions to which it committed itself at a follow-up meeting of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, and on other occasions. Canada will do everything it can to encourage such developments.

Mr. Speaker, it is now 30 years since an administration led by the late John Diefenbaker made a decision to change the terms of union which joined Newfoundland and Canada
Adjournment Debate
back in 1949. That decision brought such a storm of protest across Newfoundland and Labrador that when the next election took place, not one single Tory MP was elected in the Province. As a result of that decision, Newfoundlanders showed all of Canada that they would not knuckle under to such a cowardly backstabbing by any federal Government, whatever the stripe.
Last week, for the second time since Confederation between Newfoundland and Canada, a Government- and it so happens it is a Tory Government once again- has displayed cowardice and weakness by giving away Newfoundland's precious stocks in order to get a mechanism for settling the boundary dispute with France.
Last week in St. John's, the gentleman from St. John's West, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Cros-bie), speaking for the Government said: "We have achieved our major objectives".
What are these objectives he claimed to have achieved last week in St. John's? On what day did he achieve them, by the way? With some sense of humour, the gentleman from St. John's decided to do this to Newfoundlanders on March 31, the fortieth anniversary of Newfoundland joining Canada.
What then were these objectives that the Minister spoke about and was therefore so happy to announce at a news conference on the very anniversary of our coming into Confederation?
First, they gave away northern cod stock. What makes that giveaway of a precious Newfoundland resource to France so grossly offensive is that the scientists have already told us that there is need for a severe reduction with disastrous consequences for jobs in fish plants and perhaps fish plant closures, and disastrous consequences for fishermen both inshore and offshore.
Not only did the gentleman from St. John's West and his buddies give away northern cod stock to France on a silver platter, but they also gave France large allocations of cod and other species on the St. Pierre Bank, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and off Labrador.
Third, on top of all that, the gentleman from St. John's West gave the French access once again to Canadian ports. They have carte blanche to come and go as they wish. They have also been given the right to board Canadian fishing vessels inside Canada's 200-mile management zone. That is where we in Newfoundland draw the line.

April 11, 1989
Adjournment Debate
When Canada won that hard fought international battle to extend its jurisdiction to 200 miles with the agreement of many countries, all countries lost the right to invade that jurisdiction, to come into that zone and to board vessels willy-nilly at their whim. Last week, of course, with this concession, all that has been changed. The French are now allowed to board these vessels.
I say to the gentleman from St. John's West that this is the biggest outrage, the most disgusting abdication of all in this so-called agreement with France achieved last week. It undoes much of the work that was done so well by one of my predecessor, the late Hon. Don Jamieson, and others back in 1977.
Not only Newfoundlanders but all Canadians should be hopping mad at the Tories for creating this dangerous and insulting precedent in last week's agreement with France. Can anyone in this House or in the country imagine what the French would do if Canadians were allowed to board their fishing vessels within a few miles of their coast?
I am not given to condoning civil disobedience. I am not that kind of person. However, I can foresee real problems arising when French inspectors try to board Canadian fishing vessels within a few miles of the Newfoundland coast or the Canadian coast generally.
It would not surprise me, nor it should surprise Members opposite, particularly the gentleman from St. John's West, if Canadian fishermen will strongly resent French inspectors snooping into their affairs, and it may only be a matter of time before there is a confrontation.
I fear that a confrontation will develop because Canada has kowtowed to France belittled itself as a nation and made itself the laughing stock of the entire world by giving the French the right to provoke, intimidate and harass our fishermen in their own territorial waters. What a complete farce.
I was completely dismayed to note in this sorry affair the willing acquiescence of Newfoundland's representative in the federal Cabinet. For that dastardly deed, for his agreement with this, for standing silently by and allowing the biggest steal in Canadian history to take place, the name of the gentleman from St. John's West will be forever associated with this giveaway and will be forever tarnished as the Newfoundlander who betrayed his province and his country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the settlement reached with France is in the best interests of the
fishermen of Atlantic Canada, especially those of the Hon. Member's own riding on the south coast of Newfoundland.
The Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) knows full well that when Canada declared a 200-mile fishing zone in 1977 France also claimed a 200-mile exclusive economic zone off the Islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. Canada has continued to maintain that France's claim to an area of jurisdiction outside the 12-mile territorial sea has no basis in international law. This conflict has created a large disputed zone which is located within an important fishing area known as 3PS.
The unresolved boundary has been Canada's number one fisheries conservation problem in 3PS, because without a resolution of the conflict or an agreement to refer the dispute to an international court for adjudication, France has taken advantage of the situation to fish excessively in 3PS. French catches went from an average of 4,000 to 5,000 tonnes annually prior to 1983, to over
25.000	tonnes in 1986.
In 1987, Canada took unilateral action to curb the French appetite for Canadian fish. All undisputed Canadian waters of 3PS were closed to French fishing, and Canadian ports were closed to French fishing vessels. France received no allocations in Canadian waters in 1988, and Canadian ports remained closed to French fishing vessels. The settlement announced on March 31 is a first and essential step in solving that conservation problem once and for all. A treaty has been entered into that will send the boundary dispute to international adjudication. A tribunal composed of five judges will declare the boundary.
When the boundary is established, this will end France's ability to overfish in disputed waters once and for all. This is critical to protect the livelihood of fishermen on the south coast of Newfoundland over the long term.
Second, under the terms of settlement, France will reduce its catches in 3PS by more than 40 per cent, from
26.000	tonnes to 15,600 tonnes in 1989. In 1990 and 1991, these French quotas will be reduced by a further 500 tonnes each year.
Third, Canada has imposed important new conservation safeguards that will allow the Government to monitor French catches in disputed waters. For the first time since 1977, France will provide regular and timely reports on catches by its vessels in the disputed zone. Equally important, Canada and France will jointly carry out a series of at-sea inspections of Canadian and French vessels operating in disputed waters.
April 11, 1989

The rollback of French fishing efforts in 3PS, plus the measures to make sure that the rollback commitment is being respected, will help protect the livelihood of fishermen on Newfoundland's south coast in the short term.
As the Fisheries Council of Canada, National Sea Products, Fisheries Products International, the Newfoundland Fishermen's Union and other representatives of the Canadian fishing industry have all said, the boundary dispute must be resolved, and Canada has
Adjournment Debate
reached the best possible settlement to achieve that objective.
On behalf of his constituents, who stand to gain the most from this agreement, the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's should also welcome this settlement. [Translation]
